That image of nullification matches the sūrah’s prepared humiliating punishment for the concealer (4:37); both spenders find their spending erased, one by withholding, the other by misdirection.

**Spending Without Belief in God or the Last Day**

Not believing in God or the Last Day does not only mean formal denial; it includes acting as though no watch is kept and no return is coming. The sūrah has insisted that God is ever Watchful (4:1), enough as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12), and ever Merciful to you (4:29). To spend for show is to act as though that watch is absent and as though the only accounting is people’s praise today. The Last Day is the other half of the same belief, because it promises that even an atom’s weight will be counted and that good will be multiplied many times over (4:40). The ostentatious spender does not trust that multiplication; he seeks immediate multiplication in reputation. That is why the verse pairs spending to be seen with disbelief in the Last Day, not only with love of praise. The sūrah has already contrasted the Gardens that flow for keeping limits (4:13) and the Fire prepared for exceeding them (4:14) and for persisting until death (4:18). The spender to be seen has chosen the audience of the market over the audience of that Day, and his deed follows the audience he chose.

**Two Failures With One Root**

Read with the previous verse, the pair forms a complete diagnosis of corrupted generosity. Stinginess withholds God’s bounty and teaches others to withhold (4:37); ostentation spends bounty but diverts its aim from God and the Last Day to people’s eyes. Both refuse the same centre: spending for God who gave the bounty and who will multiply it on a Day that is coming. The sūrah has shown the correct centre repeatedly: give women dowries graciously as a free gift (4:4), return the orphan’s wealth with witnesses under God as Reckoner (4:6), divide after debts and gifts within limits watched by the Witness (4:33), trade by mutual consent under the ever Merciful (4:29). Ask God for bounty rather than crave another’s (4:32). Each act is done with God and the Last Day in view, even when the transaction is small. Ostentatious spending may mimic those acts in form — a gift to a relative, a provision to a bystander, a trade that looks consensual — but the sūrah distinguishes by audience. If the audience is people, the act is with Satan as *qarīn*; if the audience is God, the act is with Him as Guardian and Helper (4:45).
verses.39:
> What harm could have come to them if they had believed in Allah and the Last Day and donated from what Allah has provided for them? And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of them

**Belief in God, Belief in the Last Day**

The pairing *āmanū bi Allāhi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri* gathers the two beliefs that correct the two corruptions. Belief in God corrects spending without Him as audience; to believe He gave the provision is to want to spend it where He sees. Belief in the Last Day corrects concealment and show, because both assume that the only return is immediate — either saved in the chest or praised in the market. The sūrah has prepared both beliefs: God is ever Watchful (4:1), enough as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing and Most Forbearing (4:12), ever Merciful to you (4:29). The Last Day is the time when a witness is brought from every community and the Messenger is brought as witness against his own (4:41), when deniers will wish to be dust and will not be able to hide anything from God (4:42). To believe those two is to spend differently today, not because wealth is less loved but because it is more understood. The one who believes that provision came from God — *mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* — sees donation as returning, not losing; the one who believes that an atom’s weight of good will be multiplied (4:40) sees withholding as the only loss.

**Donated From What Allah Provided**

The phrase *mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* — from what Allah provided — was stressed as both the source and the limit of donation. The wealth proposed for spending is not an alien exaction but a portion of what was already given as *faḍl* — bounty — the same bounty the stingy concealed (4:37) and that others were told to ask for rather than crave (4:32). The Qur’an elsewhere says *“spend from what We have provided you before a Day comes where there is no trade”* (2:254), and the same urgency underlies this question. To donate from what was provided is to acknowledge receipt. That acknowledgment is itself worship, as the sūrah opened the ethic of kindness with *“worship Allah and associate none with Him, and be kind”* (4:36). Donation without belief, as in ostentation, is activity without worship; withholding with concealment is worship of wealth; donation *mimmā razaqa* with belief is worship that includes wealth. The amount is not specified — *mimmā* — from what, some of what — leaving room for the small provision for bystanders at distribution (4:8), the fair provision for a poor guardian (4:6), the gracious dowry (4:4), and trade by mutual consent (4:29). Each is a form of spending from what was provided.

**And Allah Has Perfect Knowledge of Them**

The closing *wa kāna Allāhu bihim ʿalīmā* — and Allah has perfect knowledge of them — answers the hidden calculation behind stinginess and ostentation. The stingy hide bounty as though God will not note the concealment; the ostentatious spend for people as though God will not see the motive. The sūrah has repeated that He is Watchful (4:1), Reckoner (4:6), Witness (4:33), and enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45); here knowledge is said to cover *them* — *bihim* — the very persons who made the choice. That knowledge does two things. For the one who feared harm from believing and donating, it reassures: the donation done with belief is known, and what is known is not lost; it will be multiplied (4:40) and brought with witnesses (4:41). For the one who thought hiding or showing would pass, it warns: the concealment and the show are also known, and on the Day when nothing can be hidden from God (4:42), the audience that was sought — people’s eyes — will not avail. The sūrah will ask *“have you not seen those given a portion of Scripture who trade it for misguidance”* (4:44) for the same reason; trading the Book for desire assumes knowledge will not follow, while the verse says it does.
verses.40:
> Indeed, Allah never wrongs ˹anyone˺—even by an atom’s weight. And if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over and will give a great reward out of His grace

**Not Even by an Atom’s Weight**

The assurance *inna Allāha lā yaẓlimu mithqāla dharratin* — indeed, Allah never wrongs even by an atom’s weight — follows the question what harm would belief and donation have done (4:39) and answers it with a measure smaller than sight. *Dharratih* — atom, speck, smallest mote seen in a sunbeam — was read as the least conceivable quantum of weight. To say God does not wrong by that weight is to say justice at the smallest scale is exact. The sūrah has been precise about small amounts before — whether inheritance is little or much (4:7), a small provision for bystanders (4:8), provision from orphan wealth without waste (4:5–6), trade by mutual consent where consent must be genuine (4:29). Here precision becomes a divine attribute. The One who appointed fractions — half, quarter, eighth, sixth, third, two-thirds — after debts and gifts (4:11–12), who required four witnesses before sanction (4:15), and who halved penalty where appropriate (4:25) is now said to weigh at a resolution finer than any human scale. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it”* (99:7–8), and this verse is the premise that makes that seeing just. Nothing is rounded away, neither a hidden donation nor a concealed bounty.

**If It Is a Good Deed, He Will Multiply It**

The second clause *wa in taku ḥasanatan yuḍāʿifhā* — and if it is a good deed, He will multiply it many times over — reverses the economy of withholding. Stinginess and ostentation (4:37–38) were both calculations that giving loses; this verse says giving gains, not one-to-one but multiplied. *Yuḍāʿif* — to double, to make many — was read as at least tenfold, as elsewhere *“whoever brings a good deed will have ten like it”* (6:160), and in other passages as seven hundredfold or without count where God wills, showing that multiplication is not a fixed rate but a generosity. The sūrah has already promised that avoiding major sins leads to covering lesser ones and a honourable entry (4:31) and that belief and donation from what was provided would have harmed no one (4:39). Multiplication explains why. A small provision offered with kind speech (4:8), a fair dowry given graciously (4:4), a just division witnessed (4:6), or a quiet trade done with genuine *tarāḍ* — mutual content (4:29) — each may seem modest, but the One who weighs atoms multiplies them.

**Justice That Is Exact and Grace That Exceeds**

The sūrah’s balance between justice and grace is stated here in a single sentence. Justice is exact — not even an atom’s weight of wrong — so that the wronged — orphan, widow, heir, neighbour — can trust that no portion is rounded away. Grace exceeds — multiplication and a great reward from His presence — so that the doer of good, even with a single sincere *ḥasanah*, can hope for more than his deed’s flat value. That pairing reflects the divine Names that have closed this section: All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26), All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12), Witness over all things (4:33), and ever Merciful to you (4:29). Knowledge ensures the atom is not missed; wisdom determines its multiplication; witness secures it; mercy adds the great reward. For the weak created weak (4:28), that pairing is the lightest of burdens: keep the major limits (4:31), believe and donate from what was provided (4:39), and know that even the smallest good is never wronged but is multiplied and crowned. The next verses will bring witnesses from every community and the Messenger as witness (4:41); what those witnesses will confirm is exactly this — that not an atom’s weight was lost, and that what was done for God was multiplied many times over and met with a great reward from His grace.
verses.41:
> So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours

**A Question That Opens the Day of Witnesses**

The verse asks *fa kayfa idhā jiʾnā min kulli ummatin bi shahīdin wa jiʾnā bika ʿalā hāʾulāʾi shahīdā* — so how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you as a witness against yours? After promises that not an atom’s weight is wronged and that good is multiplied (4:40), and after the offer to cover lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31), the sūrah turns to the Day when those promises are seen. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ is then brought as witness over his own community — the one addressed throughout al-Nisāʾ with *yā ayyuhā al-nās* (4:1) and *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* (4:29). The Qur’an elsewhere says *“We have made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over people and the Messenger may be witness over you”* (2:143), showing that witness is both a burden and a honour.

**Every Community With Its Witness**

The phrase *min kulli ummatin bi shahīdin* was read as each community brought with its messenger who will confirm the message delivered. The sūrah has detailed what that message contained in this context: creation from a single soul and guarding womb-ties (4:1), returning orphan wealth with witnesses (4:6), honouring obligatory shares after debts (4:11–12), guarding marriage through dowries and chastity (4:4, 4:24), and forbidding devouring by falsehood (4:29). On the Day, the question will be whether those limits were kept. The witness from each community will speak not from hearsay but from presence, as one who lived among his people and warned them. The scene therefore mirrors the sūrah’s insistence that human witnesses secure handovers (4:6) and that God is Witness over all things (4:33). What was done with witnesses on earth — the estate divided, the dowry given, the trade made by mutual consent — will be confirmed by the greater witnesses who saw the community as a whole. The Qur’an elsewhere says that disbelievers will wish their messengers had never been sent, but here the messengers’ presence is the proof that the community was not left without clear guidance (4:26).

**A Scene That Holds Atom’s Weight and Great Reward Together**

The verse follows the assurance that not an atom’s weight is wronged and that good is multiplied with a great reward from grace (4:40), and it shows where that assurance is displayed. The witnesses are brought because accounting must be seen to be exact. The atom’s weight that was never wronged in the estate division, the dowry left where it was given despite a heap of gold (4:20), the small provision offered with kind speech (4:8) — all will appear not as hidden details but as recorded deeds with witnesses. The promise of multiplication and grace and the warning of Fire that is easy for God (4:30) are both made credible by the court that this verse opens. Without witnesses, the promises could feel distant; with prophets and with the Prophet ﷺ as witnesses, the promises become a scene the reader can picture and therefore prepare for. The sūrah has already said that God is ever Watchful (4:1) and enough as Reckoner (4:6) and Helper (4:45); this verse is that watch and reckoning made visible, with human witnesses who lived the law brought to confirm.
verses.42:
> On that Day, those who denied ˹Allah˺ and disobeyed the Messenger will wish they were reduced to dust. And they will never be able to hide anything from Allah

**Those Who Denied and Disobeyed the Messenger**

The pairing *kafarū wa ʿaṣaw al-rasūla* gathers two groups and two modes. *Kafarū* — denied — covers those who covered the bounty and the sign, as the stingy concealed what God gave and the ostentatious spent for eyes without belief (4:37–38). *ʿAṣaw al-rasūla* — disobeyed the Messenger — covers those who heard the shares, the bar on reclaiming dowries, and the command to appoint mediators yet followed desires to deviate greatly (4:27). The sūrah has linked disbelief and disobedience throughout: *“whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and exceeds His limits will be cast into Fire”* (4:14), *“whoever takes Satan as associate, what an evil associate”* (4:38) where the associate’s counsel is disobedience. *“obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you, and refer disputes to them”* (4:59). The Day groups them because their outcome converges.

**And They Will Never Be Able to Hide Anything from Allah**

The clause *wa lā yaktumūna Allāha ḥadīthā* — and they will never be able to hide anything from Allah — closes the scene with knowledge. *Ḥadīth* — speech, statement, narration — was read as any statement they might wish to hide — the hidden mixing of orphan wealth (4:2), the pressured dowry return (4:19–20), the fraudulent trade (4:29), the words of distortion such as *“we hear and we disobey”* (4:46). On the Day when witnesses are brought (4:41), hiding fails because the One who is ever Watchful (4:1), enough as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), and All-Knowing, All-Aware (4:35) is the One to whom no *ḥadīth* is concealed. The Qur’an elsewhere says that hands, feet, and skin will testify and that records will not leave small or great except counted. Here the same certainty is stated simply: no hiding. The sūrah has warned that God has perfect knowledge of them (4:39) and that He never wrongs even by an atom’s weight but multiplies good (4:40); that atom-level accounting now becomes the reason no speech can be hidden. What was concealed as bounty (4:37) will be known as concealed; what was spent for show (4:38) will be known as shown. The Day does not need new evidence; it reveals what perfect knowledge already contained.

**A Scene That Holds the Sūrah’s Warnings Together**

Read with 4:41, this verse completes the witness tableau that the sūrah will use for its pivot to purification and to the Children of the Book. The court is assembled with a witness from every community and the Prophet ﷺ over his own; those who denied and disobeyed are present and wish to be levelled; no speech can be hidden from God. The tableau therefore gathers the three threads that have run together: God’s will to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27), the limits whose keeping is obedience and whose exceeding is Fire (4:13–14, 4:30), and the mercy that covers lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31). Those who kept the major limits and turned soon after ignorance (4:17) will stand differently under that sky than those who persisted until death was present (4:18). The verse does not name the believers’ recompense here; it leaves their standing implied by the sūrah’s larger pattern of honourable entry (4:31) and vast shade with pure spouses (4:57). For the deniers and disobedient, the recompense is named as a wish that cannot be granted and a concealment that cannot be kept, which is itself a form of exposure. The Day that begins with how will it be ends here with they will wish they were dust, showing that the community’s choice between clarity and desire, made in matters as small as a sixth and as serious as *shirk*, will have a weight that even the earth cannot cover.

The Qur’an elsewhere says that the disbeliever will say *“O would that I were dust”* (78:40), and this verse places that cry at the specific court of witnesses the previous verse opened.
verses.43:
> O believers! Do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say, nor in a state of ˹full˺ impurity—unless you merely pass through ˹the mosque˺—until you have bathed. But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth, wiping your faces and hands. And Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

**Prayer Guarded by Awareness**

The verse opens with a direct address — *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā taqrabū al-ṣalāta wa antum sukārā ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn* — O believers, do not approach prayer while intoxicated until you are aware of what you say. The condition *ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn* — until you know what you are saying — makes awareness the threshold for standing in prayer. Prayer in the Qur’an is described as remembrance, recitation, and supplication where the heart and tongue must align; intoxication removes that alignment. Early reports place this verse in the Medinan period before the full prohibition of wine, when drinking remained common and a person might come to prayer with speech blurred. The sūrah therefore holds the line at the meeting point of worship and heedlessness: do not bring the state that empties words to the act that depends on words. The Qur’an elsewhere says that wine has benefit and great sin and that sin outweighs benefit (2:219), and later it will say *“wine, gambling, idols, and fortune arrows are defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid them entirely”* (5:90). This verse is the middle step in that gradual legislation, keeping prayer clear while the community is being prepared for the final bar.

**Earth as Purifier Where Water Is Absent**

The choice of *ṣaʿīd ṭayyib* — clean earth, high ground, dust — as purifier was noted for its availability. Earth is where people stand, whether healthy or ill, at home or on a journey; to make it a means of purification is to make purification available in the very place where water fails. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“Allah does not wish to place hardship upon you, but to purify you and complete His favour upon you”* (5:6), and this verse is the classic instance. The sūrah has already said God wills to make things clear and to lighten burdens (4:26–28); here clarity and lightening meet in a single rite: clear instruction about when not to approach, and a lightened way to be ready when water is absent. The wiping of face and hands — the most visible parts — also carries meaning beyond convenience. The face is the direction of prayer and the site of prostration; the hands are the instruments of trade and giving that the sūrah has guarded from devouring by falsehood (4:29). To wipe both with clean earth is to mark the whole person — seeing and doing — as ready, even where full bathing is not possible.

**Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving Over Slip and Need**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* — and Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving — matches the two bars and the one concession. *ʿAfuww* — pardoning, effacing — was read as wiping out the trace, as earth wipes the requirement of water. *Ghafūr* — forgiving, covering — as covering the shortfall where the believer tried to prepare but was hindered by illness, travel, or lack. The sūrah has closed similar lightenings with Forgiving, Merciful (4:25) and with clear, wise guidance (4:26); here the pardon covers both the intoxicated person who once approached without knowing what he said before the final prohibition, and the junub person who feared prayer would be lost where water was absent. The gradual bar on wine shows *ʿafw* in legislation itself: the community was not condemned as though it had always known the final rule, but was taught until *ḥattā taʿlamū* — until you know what you are saying — became the standard for standing.

**A Verse That Holds Worship and Weakness Together**

Placed between the scene of witnesses and dust (4:41–42) and the exposure of those who trade guidance for misguidance (4:44), this verse holds worship and weakness together without loosening either. In that double training, the sūrah’s larger purpose becomes visible again: to make things clear, to guide to noble ways, to turn in mercy, and to lighten because the human was created weak (4:26–28).
verses.44:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet trade it for misguidance and wish to see you deviate from the ˹Right˺ Path

**A Portion of the Book, Traded Away**
The verse asks the Prophet to look at a group who had been given a share of the earlier scriptures and then bought misguidance with it, and who wanted to see the believers drift off the straight path. The Arabic picture is a purchase: they held guidance and paid it away for straying. Commentators connect the verse with Jewish scholars in Madinah who knew the descriptions of the coming Prophet in their own books, hid what they knew, or charged for their reading of it, and counselled doubt. The charge in the verse is wider than those men: anyone given a share of the Book who would rather keep his standing than let people see the truth has made the same trade.

**The Wish Behind the Trade**
The verse joins the trade to a wish. They do not simply go astray themselves; they want the believers to leave the road. The same desire is named a few verses earlier, where the Book says that those who follow their own desires wish to see the believers wander far off the path (4:27). The road the sūrah keeps describing is concrete: marriage entered honestly with wealth rather than with appetite (4:24), trade by consent and not by devouring other people's money with falsehood (4:29), and no craving after the position God has given others (4:32). To want people off that road is to want them loose from the rules that protect the weak.

**What They Chose Instead**
The verse is also a contrast with three earlier pictures. There were the misers who hold back what God has given them and urge others to be miserly too (4:37), and the ones who give to be seen and do not believe in God or the last day (4:38). The Book answers them with a question: what harm would it have done them to believe and to give from what God provided (4:39), when God multiplies even an atom's weight of good and adds a great reward (4:40)? The sūrah has also reminded them of the cleanliness and attention it asks even in ordinary duty (4:43), and it has told the Prophet that God knows best who his enemies are, and that God is enough as guardian and helper (4:45). The verse closes with the contrast it has been building: the men bought straying with a book that could have guided them, and the Messenger was told to leave them to the One who sees (4:47). The sūrah has said what God wants instead of this trading: He wants to make matters clear to people, to guide them and to accept the repentance of those who turn back (4:26).
verses.45:
> Allah knows best who your enemies are! And Allah is sufficient as a Guardian, and He is sufficient as a Helper

**Allah Knows Best Who Your Enemies Are**

The statement *wa Allāhu aʿlamu bi aʿdāʾikum* — and Allah knows best who your enemies are — follows the exposure of those who were given a portion of the Book yet trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate (4:44). The community in Madinah lived among groups whose enmity was not always declared as open battle; some concealed it behind counsel, distorted phrasing, and the wish to mislead. The sūrah has just said those sellers wish you to deviate from the path (4:44) and earlier that those who follow desires wish you to swerve greatly (4:27). To know the enemy in that setting is not to know only the battlefield opponent but to know the whisperer who trades guidance for influence. *Aʿlamu* — knows best — was read as both comfort and warning. Comfort, because the believer need not uncover every hidden motive; the One who is ever Watchful (4:1), Witness over all things (4:33), and All-Knowing, All-Aware (4:35) already knows. Warning, because the believer should not mistake a wish to misguide for friendship. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“He knows the treachery of eyes and what breasts conceal,”* and that knowledge is the background to naming enemies here without needing to list each name.

**Sufficient as Guardian**

The reassurance *wa kafā bi Allāhi waliyyā* — and Allah is enough as a Guardian — addresses the fear that follows knowledge of enmity. *Walī* — guardian, protector, near ally — was explained as the one who takes charge of affairs, who stands over the ward as a guardian stands over the orphan’s wealth with witnessing and reckoning (4:6). The sūrah has built the image of guardianship from the first verse — *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1) — through debt and gift order, marriage law, and the promise that not an atom’s weight is wronged but good is multiplied (4:40). To say He is enough as *Walī* is to say that those trusts need no other guarantor where enmity is present. Those who trade the Book for misguidance may wish you to deviate, but the Guardian who willed to make things clear and to guide to noble ways (4:26) is enough to keep the path clear. The phrase *kafā bi* — enough is — appears after detailed legislation to steady those who must apply it under pressure. A judge who must refuse a gift that harms heirs (4:12), a guardian who must return an orphan’s wealth with witnesses, or a family that must appoint mediators (4:35) each faces pressure from those who benefit from blur; sufficiency as Guardian tells them the law has a Keeper beyond people.

**Knowledge, Guardianship, and Help Together**

The three clauses belong together: He knows enemies, He suffices as Guardian, He suffices as Helper. Knowledge without guardianship would leave the believer exposed; guardianship without help would leave him watched but not aided. The sūrah’s earlier Names joined knowledge with wisdom (4:11, 4:26), knowledge with forbearance (4:12), and knowledge with awareness (4:35); here knowledge is joined with sufficiency. That sufficiency was already implied when the sūrah said *“you are from one another”* (4:25) and *“you know not which are nearer to you in benefit”* (4:11), both statements that ask the believer to trust the apportioning of the One who knows. In a city where portions of Scripture were traded and where wording was twisted — *“we hear and disobey,” “herd us”* with a twist (4:46) — the believer might doubt whether clarity can survive distortion. The verse answers that clarity survives because its Guardian is enough; the believers’ task is not to outwit every distortion but to hold the Book, refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger (4:59), and trust the Helper who multiplies an atom’s weight of good (4:40).

The sūrah has shown help as turning toward you when you turn (4:27–28) and as lightening because you were created weak (4:28).
verses.46:
> Some Jews take words out of context and say, “We listen and we disobey,” “Hear! May you never hear,” and “Râ’ina!” [Herd us!]—playing with words and discrediting the faith. Had they said ˹courteously˺, “We hear and obey,” “Listen to us,” and “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] it would have been better for them and more proper. Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few

**Three Sayings That Twist Courtesy Into Contempt**

*We listen and we disobey* was heard as a public declaration that replaces obedience with defiance while claiming to have listened, preserving the form of reception and emptying it. *Hear, may you never hear* was read as a curse to the Prophet ﷺ delivered as though it were a greeting, a double tongue that could be denied as mishearing. *Rāʿinā* was the most subtle, because the call *rāʿinā* — look at us, tend to us — sounds like *unẓurnā* but carries a different root that can be stretched to mean *rāʿi* — foolish, shepherd to be herded — and was used with a drawl and wink to insult while seeming to ask for attention. The Qur’an elsewhere tells believers *“do not say rāʿinā but say unẓurnā and listen”* (2:104), replacing the ambiguous with the clear to close the opening for mockery. The sūrah’s concern for clarity — *Allah wills to make things clear* (4:26) — is therefore protected at the level of vocabulary. A single word’s tilt can tilt the community’s hearing, which is why the verse details the tilt rather than summarizing it.

**What They Could Have Said**

The verse offers the straight alternative: *wa law annahum qālū samīʿnā wa aṭaʿnā wa asmaʿ wa anẓurnā la kāna khayran lahum wa aqwam* — had they said we hear and obey, listen to us. Tend to us, it would have been better for them and more proper. *Samīʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — we hear and obey — was the believers’ reply at *“we hear and we obey”* elsewhere, a phrase that gathers hearing and action together. *Ismaʿ* — listen — without the curse, and *unẓurnā* — tend to us — with the unambiguous root, would have secured the request without the twist. The pair *khayran lahum wa aqwam* — better for them and more proper, more upright — shows that straight speech is both more beneficial and more correctly aimed — *aqwam* — straighter, like an arrow that flies true. The sūrah has praised *qawlan maʿrūfā* — kind speech at distribution (4:5, 4:8) — and *qawlan sadīdā* — straight, true speech (4:9), and here it shows what crooked speech sounds like and what straight speech would have been. The difference is not eloquence but sincerity. A community that learns to say *we hear and obey* will also learn to handle deposits, shares, and dowries as heard and obeyed limits; a community that says *we hear and disobey* will treat limits as sounds to be played with.

**Condemned for Disbelief — Faith Except for a Few**

The closing *wa lākin laʿanahumu Allāhu bi kufrihim fa lā yuʾminūna illā qalīlā* — Allah has condemned them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except for a few — ties distortion to its root. *Laʿn* — to expel from mercy, to condemn — was read as the consequence of covering the bounty and trading it (4:37, 4:44). Because they distorted, they were condemned, and because they were condemned for persistent disbelief, the habit of faith left them, except for a few who turned, such as those who accepted the Prophet ﷺ and whose belief the sūrah elsewhere acknowledges. The clause *illā qalīlan* — except a little, except a few — keeps the door ajar for the individual. The condemnation is not ethnic fate but response to a chosen practice of turning words after their places; the few who said *we hear and obey* were not condemned, which is why belief remained possible for them. The sūrah has already said that God forgives anything less than association with Him for whomever He wills (4:48) and that a painful punishment is prepared for those who persist until death says now I repent (4:18); here the same structure applies in the domain of speech. Persistent twisting hardens into disbelief that makes belief rare, while a straight word at the start — *unẓurnā* instead of *rāʿinā* — would have been better and more proper and would have kept the way open.
verses.47:
> O you who were given the Book! Believe in what We have revealed—confirming your own Scriptures—before We wipe out ˹your˺ faces, turning them backwards, or We condemn the defiant as We did to the Sabbath-breakers. And Allah’s command is always executed

**The Sabbath-Breakers as Precedent**

The reference to the Sabbath-breakers was read as more than a scare; it was a legal analogy. The Sabbath limit was a *ḥadd* — a divine boundary — like the inheritance limits called *ḥudūd* (4:13–14) and the marriage bars (4:22–23). Those who broke it by setting nets before the Sabbath and collecting after, claiming they had not fished on the day, were condemned because the stratagem kept the form while breaking the substance, much as *rāʿinā* kept the sound of *unẓurnā* while meaning insult. The sūrah has guarded against similar stratagems with wealth: hasty consumption before the orphan grows (4:6), gifts that harm heirs (4:12), and devouring by falsehood in trade (4:29). Each uses a form that looks lawful while its substance is taking. To warn with the Sabbath-breakers is to say that God’s limits are not defeated by wordplay. The condemnation — *laʿn* — that expels from mercy is the same word used for those condemned for distortion and disbelief (4:46), tying the two groups together. What was done to those who broke a temporal limit would be done to those who break the confirming Book’s limit, because the limit’s Owner is the same.

**And Allah’s Command Is Always Executed**

The closing *wa kāna amru Allāhi mafʿūlā* — and Allah’s command is always executed — seals the warning with inevitability. *Amr* — command, affair — was read as both decree and order; what He commands to be, is, and what He warns will happen if belief is refused will not be delayed by anyone’s plan. The sūrah has said that God never wrongs even by an atom’s weight but multiplies good (4:40) and that He has perfect knowledge of them (4:39); that knowledge now becomes capability, as the command that is executed shows. The phrase follows the double threat — wiping faces or condemning as the Sabbath-breakers — to make clear that neither is bluster. The community that heard *“have you not seen those who trade a portion for misguidance”* (4:44) might have thought the traders would simply persist without consequence; this verse says persistence ends in an executed command. Yet the call before the threat remains belief — *āminū* — which is still possible while the warning is given. The sūrah’s pattern of clarity before sanction — limits named, then Gardens and Fire named (4:13–14) — is kept: the confirming Book is named, the confirmation explained, the threat described, and the command’s execution guaranteed, so that choice is made with open eyes.

**A Call That Confirms Rather Than Cancels**

Read after the diagnosis of twisted phrases, this verse is the sūrah’s invitation to the very group diagnosed: believe in what confirms your own. It does not ask those given the Book to erase their history; it asks them to see its fulfilment. The limits they were given — about property, family, and worship — are made clear again and lightened because humankind was created weak (4:28); the Book that makes them clear is the same that confirms. To refuse that confirmation while trading the portion they have (4:44) is to turn faces away from the direction they were meant to face. The executed command will then do what their own turning refused: turn them backward. The sūrah leaves the path open before that execution — believe now — because the One who warns is also the One who said *“Allah wishes to turn to you in grace”* (4:27) and *“and Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving”* (4:43). The faces that could be wiped can instead be turned forward in belief, where the confirming Book is recognized and the warning is no longer needed.
verses.48:
> Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating others with Him ˹in worship˺, but forgives anything else of whoever He wills. And whoever associates others with Allah has indeed committed a grave sin

**A Boundary That Does Not Move**

The statement *inna Allāha lā yaghfiru a yushraka bihi wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* — indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him. Forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills — places one sin outside the general amnesty that the sūrah has been offering for lesser faults. The previous promise *“if you avoid major sins, We will cover your lesser misdeeds and admit you to honour”* (4:31) and the assurance that repentance soon after ignorance is accepted (4:17) could be heard as though every fault, if deferred, would eventually be covered. This verse corrects that hearing by naming the limit. *Shirk* — associating others with God in worship, devotion, or ultimate trust — is not a lesser fault to be covered by avoidance of other majors; it is the breach of the first command the sūrah gave after its family laws: *“worship Allah and associate none with Him”* (4:36). The verse therefore draws a line that the ethic of *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, neighbours, and travellers circles around but does not cross. All else — *mā dūna dhālika* — anything below that — remains under divine will to forgive, which the sūrah has described as perfect knowledge of them (4:39), never wronging by an atom’s weight but multiplying good (4:40), and ever-pardoning, ever-forgiving (4:43).

**Forgives Anything Else of Whoever He Wills**

The phrase *wa yaghfiru mā dūna dhālika li man yashāʾ* was read as vast scope. *Mā dūna* — what is below, less than — covers every sin that is not *shirk*, from consuming orphan wealth (4:10) to devouring by falsehood (4:29) to illicit intercourse (4:15–16), provided the conditions for forgiveness elsewhere are met — repentance soon after ignorance (4:17) rather than deferral until death is present (4:18). Avoidance of persistence as habit. *Li man yashāʾ* — for whomever He wills — was stressed as showing forgiveness is not automatic; it is will, knowledge, and wisdom together, as the sūrah closes similar verses with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26, 4:11) and All-Knowing, Most Forbearing (4:12). The will to forgive those who turn is real — *“Allah wishes to turn to you in grace”* (4:27) and to lighten because you are weak (4:28) — but it remains His will, not a claim any sinner can demand. That balance keeps the community from presumptuous despair and from presumptuous guarantee. A person who has committed a major sin that is not *shirk* is not told forgiveness is impossible; he is told it is possible for whomever God wills, and that will is known to be merciful to those who avoid the major and ask for bounty (4:32, 4:39).

Placed after the warning that faces could be wiped or the defiant condemned like Sabbath-breakers (4:47), this verse explains the theology behind that severity. Wiping faces and *laʿn* were not arbitrary penalties for wordplay; they were responses to disbelief that includes association — taking scholars, desires, or idols as arbiters beside God. The sūrah will go on to describe those who believe in idols and false gods and claim they guide better than believers (4:51), showing the live form of association the verse addresses. By naming the unforgiven sin here, the sūrah clarifies the path back: believe in what was revealed confirming your own (4:47), worship without association and be kind to parents and others (4:36), and ask God for bounty rather than crave another’s (4:32). Those who do so remain under *li man yashāʾ* — the will that forgives what is below *shirk* — where soon repentance (4:17) and avoidance of major sins (4:31) bring covering. Those who persist in association have fabricated the one lie that covers over the source of forgiveness itself, which is why it is not forgiven when held to death.
verses.49:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who ˹falsely˺ elevate themselves? It is Allah who elevates whoever He wills. And none will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone

**It Is Allah Who Elevates Whoever He Wills**

The correction *bali Allāhu yuzakkī man yashāʾ* — rather, it is Allah who elevates whoever He wills — returns the act of purification to its Owner. *Yuzakkī* — to purify, to elevate, to cause to grow — is God’s act, not a status claimed by speech. The sūrah has shown that purification comes through His ways: making things clear (4:26), guiding to noble ways, turning toward you and lightening because you are weak (4:26–28), covering lesser faults when major sins are avoided (4:31), and accepting soon repentance for ignorance (4:17). To claim purity without that path is to claim the fruit without the root. *Man yashāʾ* — whoever He wills — was stressed as will joined to knowledge and wisdom, as the sūrah closes similar verses with All-Knowing, All-Wise (4:26) and Most Forbearing (4:12). The will to purify is not arbitrary; it follows the pattern the sūrah has taught: the one who worships without association and is kind to parents, orphans, neighbours. Travellers (4:36), who gives dowries graciously (4:4), who trades by mutual consent (4:29), and who asks God for bounty rather than craves another’s (4:32) is the one God elevates. The self-praiser who conceals bounty and promotes stinginess (4:37) is not elevated by his own claim, because the elevation he seeks is in people’s eyes, not before the One who sees.

**Not Even by the Width of a Date Thread**

The assurance *wa lā yuẓlamūna fatīlā* — and none will be wronged even by the width of the thread of a date stone — follows the correction to calm both hope and fear. *Fatīl* — the thin thread in the groove of a date pit — was read alongside *naqīr* — speck on a date stone (4:53) — and *qiṭmīr* — film on a date pit elsewhere — as images of the smallest amount. The sūrah has used such measures to stress precision: *“whether it is little or much”* inheritance must be shared (4:7), a small provision for bystanders with kind speech (4:8), an atom’s weight never wronged but multiplied (4:40), and self-elevation as a *farīyah* — fabrication — that is a blatant sin (4:50). The Qur’an elsewhere says that on the Day when a witness is brought and no speech can be hidden (4:41–42), the record will not leave small or great except counted.

**A Community Invited to Be Purified, Not to Claim Purity**

Placed between the grave sin of association (4:48) and the blatant fabrication of lies against God (4:50), this verse steadies the community between two traps: despair that no one can be pure and presumption that some already are by birth. The sūrah’s answer is that purity is given, not taken, and that it is given without wrong by even a thread. The poor guardian who took only what is fair (4:6), the heir who kept limits and was promised Gardens (4:13), the couple who sought mediators desiring reconciliation and found God bringing harmony (4:35). The spender who believed and donated from what was provided (4:39) — each may be elevated, not because they claimed it but because God wills it and does not wrong by a *fatīl*. The question have you not seen is therefore both exposure and invitation. Have you not seen the self-praisers? Do not be them. And have you not seen that the only true elevation is God’s act? Ask Him for it, as the verse before invited *ask Allah for His bounty* (4:32), and let Him purify you on the Day when not a thread’s width is missed. The self-declared pure will find their claim weighs less than a *fatīl*; the quietly purified will find their atom multiplied many times over.

The Qur’an elsewhere says *“do not claim purity for yourselves; He knows best who is mindful”* (53:32), and this verse is the sūrah’s instance, placed where self-elevation was being used to excuse word distortion and trade of the Book.
verses.50:
> See how they fabricate lies against Allah—this alone is a blatant sin

**See How They Fabricate**

The command *unẓur kayfa yaftarūna ʿalā Allāhi al-kadhib* — see how they fabricate lies against Allah — directs the gaze to a practice just described: declaring themselves pure (4:49) while Allah alone purifies whomever He wills without wronging by a thread. *Iftarā* — to fabricate, to cut out a lie and present it as truth — was read as inventing a claim and attaching God’s Name to it, saying God has approved what He has not. In the Madinan context that fabrication took forms the sūrah has traced: that only one group will enter the Garden, that God loves them because of lineage, that distorted words — *we hear and disobey* veiled as obedience (4:46) — represent His intent, or that trading a portion of the Book for misguidance (4:44) is guidance. The verb *yaftarūna* suggests ongoing work; the lie is not a slip but a craft, repeated until it feels like doctrine. The sūrah elsewhere says *“whoever associates with Allah has fabricated a grave sin”* (4:48), showing that *shirk* is the root fabrication; this verse shows the branch that grows from self-purification — the claim that God has already endorsed the claimant, which is a lie against Him.

**Fabrication After Self-Elevation**

The link to the previous verse is direct. Those who elevate themselves — *yuzakkūna anfusahum* (4:49) — must supply a story for why they are elevated; the story becomes a lie against God — He told us we are pure, He will not punish us, He favours our lineage. The sūrah elsewhere records such stories: *“we are God’s children and beloved”* and *“none will enter the Garden except Jews or Christians.”* Each attributes to God a promise He did not make. The earlier warning that no one will be wronged by even a thread — *fatīl* — (4:49) and by even a speck on a date stone — *naqīr* — (4:53) is the measure that exposes the fabrication. A community where an atom’s weight is not wronged (4:40) cannot also have a community where purity is assigned by birth without deed, because the second claim would wrong every doer whose atom was counted. The fabrication therefore contradicts the sūrah’s ethic of deed-based shares — *men according to what they earned and women according to what they earned* (4:32) — and the ethic of asking God for bounty (4:32) rather than claiming it.

**A Sin That Is Clear Without Further Evidence**

To call the fabrication *ithman mubīnan* — a blatant sin — is to say it is evident without needing a hidden motive to be uncovered. The lie is blatant because the Book that confirms (4:47) is present to compare, because the Witness over all things (4:33) is invoked, and because the atom’s weight that is never wronged is the standard that shows the lie’s excess. Early authorities noted that the sūrah makes this sin visible by its own method: it quotes the distorted phrases — *we hear and disobey, herd us* — (4:46) and then quotes the straight phrases — *we hear and obey, tend to us* — so the fabrication can be heard. Here it quotes the act of self-elevation and then quotes the correction — *Allah purifies whomever He wills* — so the sin’s clarity is audible as well. The verse does not detail the punishment here, as it did for devouring orphan wealth (4:10) or exceeding limits (4:14), because *kafā bihi* — enough is it — already tells the reader that this fabrication alone suffices to be counted as grave. The next verses will add the broader idolatry where those given a portion of the Book reassure disbelievers they are better guided than believers (4:51), showing how one fabrication leads to another, but this verse holds the focus on the lie against God as enough on its own.
verses.51:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who were given a portion of the Scriptures yet believe in idols and false gods and reassure the disbelievers that they are better guided than the believers

**Belief in Jibt and Ṭāghūt After a Portion of the Book**

The phrase *yuʾminūna bi al-jibti wa al-ṭāghūt* was read as more than consulting an idol for a day; it is belief — *īmān* — misdirected. The portion of the Book taught *tawḥīd* — worship without partner — and taught that good is multiplied and that even an atom’s weight is not wronged (4:40). To give belief to *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* is to give that trust to what cannot weigh or multiply, to a false judge the believers were commanded to reject (4:60). Early commentators listed *jibt* as sorcery, idols, and whoever is followed in disobedience. *ṭāghūt* as the head of falsehood who is obeyed beyond his limit, tying both to the later warning *“have you not seen those who claim belief yet seek judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject, and Satan desires to lead them farther away”* (4:60). Here the same pattern appears at the level of doctrine: those given the Book, whose portion should have taught rejection of *ṭāghūt*, become its believers, and in that belief they validate the disbelievers’ path. The reversal is complete: the teachers of *tawḥīd* become teachers that *shirk* is better guided.

**Why the Question Exposes the Seller**

The question *a lam tara* does not ask the Prophet ﷺ for news he lacks; it asks the community to see what the sellers have become. By naming the sellers as those given a portion, the verse reminds them that knowledge came first; unbelief in idols was not too high for them, because they had the Book that forbade it. To believe in *jibt* after that is chosen, not inherited, which is why the next verse says *they are the ones condemned by Allah* (4:52). The sūrah has already placed the unforgiven sin as *shirk* (4:48) and the blatant sin as fabricating lies against God (4:50); belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and the reassurance to polytheists gather both. The reassurance fabricates that disbelief is guidance, and the belief brings *shirk* where *tawḥīd* was taught. The community that was told *“do not crave what Allah gave some over others but ask Him for bounty”* (4:32) and *“what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided”* (4:39) is here shown the opposite trade: those who had a portion did not ask for more bounty from God. They gave belief to idols and told others that the better path is the one God said not to forgive if held to death.

**A Warning Not to Sell Guidance for Alliance**

Placed between the blatant fabrication (4:50) and the condemnation with no helper (4:52), this verse warns the believers not to imitate the sellers. A portion of the Book — now the Qur’an — has also been given to them; to use it to reassure those who deny God and disobey the Messenger that they are better guided would be to repeat the same sale. The sūrah will soon command *“return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness”* (4:58) and *“obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. Refer disputes to them”* (4:59), showing where guidance is to be sought — not from *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* but from the Book and the Messenger. To have been given a portion and then to believe in false gods and to call the disbeliever better guided is to fail that referral at its first step. The verse therefore asks have you not seen so that the believers see and do not become like those who, having been given a share of guidance, believed in the very thing the guidance came to remove, and then told others that the removed thing guides better.
verses.52:
> It is they who have been condemned by Allah. And whoever is condemned by Allah will have no helper

**Condemned by Allah**

The verse states *ulāʾika alladhīna laʿanahumu Allāh* — it is they who have been condemned by Allah — referring to those described just before as given a portion of the Scriptures yet believing in idols and false gods and reassuring disbelievers they are better guided than believers (4:51). *Laʿn* — to condemn, to expel from mercy — was read as God’s declaration that the offender is removed from His special mercy, the mercy that elsewhere is promised as turning toward you and lightening burdens because you were created weak (4:26–28). The sūrah has used *laʿn* for those who distort words and say *“we hear and disobey”* (4:46) and for the threat before faces are wiped or the defiant condemned like Sabbath-breakers (4:47). Here condemnation is not a prediction but a status: they have been condemned. The reason gathers the sequence: they were given a portion of the Book, they traded it for misguidance and wished believers to deviate (4:44), they played with words to discredit faith (4:46), they were invited to believe in what confirms their own before a severe transformation (4:47), they were warned that *shirk* is not forgiven when held to death while what is below it may be forgiven for whomever God wills (4:48), yet they chose belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and told polytheists they were better guided. To be condemned after that series is not arbitrary; it is the name for persisting in the trade after the price and the alternative were made clear.

**No Helper Where Help Is Most Needed**

The phrase *lan tajida lahu naṣīrā* — you will never find for him a helper — was read as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and to any listener, as though to say look for a helper for them and you will not find one. That search was imagined on the Day when witnesses are brought (4:41), when wealth that was concealed (4:37) and speech that was distorted (4:46) and idols that were believed (4:51) each fail to intercede. The sūrah has repeatedly contrasted two companionships: the evil associate — Satan as *qarīn* — and the enough Guardian and Helper — God Himself (4:45). To be condemned is to be left with the first and to lose the second. The sūrah will soon ask *“do they have shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not give a speck”* (4:53) and *“do they envy people for God’s bounties?”* (4:54), showing that those with no share of kingdom and with envy as motive cannot help even themselves, let alone another. The verse therefore answers the alliance the sellers sought when they reassured polytheists.

**A Verse That Steadies the Believers’ Trust**

Between the exposure of belief in false gods (4:51) and the question about kingdom shares (4:53), this short verse steadies the believers’ trust. The community that was told to refer disputes to Allah and the Messenger (4:59) and to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58) might fear that alliances of sellers of misguidance and polytheists will overwhelm them. The verse says the calculus is simpler: whoever God condemns will have no helper, and God knows best who enemies are and suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). The sūrah has already shown that God never wrongs even by an atom’s weight but multiplies good many times over (4:40), and that He will cover lesser faults for those who avoid major sins (4:31). Those promises remain for the believers who keep limits. For the condemned, the opposite promise holds: no helper will appear to cover the *shirk* that is not forgiven when held to death (4:48) or the fabricated lie against God that is enough as blatant sin (4:50). The verse’s brevity matches its function. After the detailed trade of a portion for *jibt* and the reassurance to disbelievers, a single sentence about condemnation and no helper tells the community where that trade ends, and whom to trust instead.
verses.53:
> Do they have control over shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone

**Do They Have Shares of the Kingdom**

The question *a lahu naṣībun min al-mulk fa idhan lā yuʾtūna al-nāsa naqīrā* — do they have control over shares of the kingdom? If so, they would not have given anyone so much as the speck on a date stone — follows the condemnation of those who believe in idols and declare polytheists better guided (4:51) and who have no helper once condemned (4:52). The sūrah now asks whether such people have any share of dominion — *naṣīb min al-mulk* — that would justify their judgment about who is better guided or their claim to distribute favour. *Mulk* — kingdom, authority, dominion — in this sūrah has appeared as God’s appointment of heirs (4:33) and as the heritage to which He multiplies reward (4:40); to have a share of it would be to have a stake in apportioning guidance, provision, and intercession. The verse denies they have any. Their portion was a share of the Book — *naṣīban min al-kitāb* (4:44, 4:51) — which they traded for misguidance; they have no share of kingdom. The Qur’an elsewhere says that if people had the treasuries of mercy, they would withhold from fear of spending, because humanity is ever stingy; this verse is that truth applied to those who claim better guidance for disbelievers. If the keys were theirs, they would not open them even a *naqīr* — the speck in the groove of a date stone.

**A Speck on a Date Stone**

The image *naqīr* — speck, small pit, the tiny dot on a date stone — joins *fatīl* — thread (4:49) — and *qiṭmīr* — film elsewhere — as measures of the smallest amount. The sūrah has used such measures to stress that God never wrongs even by an atom’s weight but multiplies good (4:40), and that none will be wronged by a thread (4:49). To say the condemned would not give even a *naqīr* is to say they are the opposite of the divine economy they claim to judge. The sellers of misguidance, by contrast, would withhold even a speck if they controlled shares, which is why they reassured disbelievers they were better guided — not from magnanimity but from stinginess toward believers, a form of *bukhl* already condemned as concealing bounty and promoting stinginess (4:37).

**Why the Question About Kingdom Follows Belief in Idols**

The sequence is deliberate. Belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51) is a claim to an alternative kingdom — a false authority whose judgment is obeyed. To ask do they have a share of the kingdom is to ask whether that false authority owns any real dominion. The answer is none. Those who take Satan as associate have an evil associate (4:38), but they have no share of *mulk* to distribute; the associate they took cannot give. The sūrah has shown true kingdom in its own domain: He appoints heirs, He sets limits — *ḥudūd* — whose keeping brings Gardens and whose crossing brings humiliating Fire (4:13–14), He brings witnesses from every community (4:41), He turns toward those who turn soon (4:17). That kingdom is not shared with those who believe in idols; it judges them. The verse therefore exposes the sellers’ boast as empty. They acted as though they could grant guidance by declaring disbelievers better guided; the verse says if guidance and kingdom were theirs to apportion, they would keep even a *naqīr* to themselves, which proves they do not have it. The only kingdom that matters — God’s — is generous to an atom and beyond, which is why belief in Him and donation from what He provided would have harmed no one (4:39).
verses.54:
> Or do they envy the people for Allah’s bounties? Indeed, We have given the descendants of Abraham the Book and wisdom, along with great authority

**Envy for Bounty Given**

The question *am yaḥsudūna al-nāsa ʿalā mā ātāhumu Allāhu min faḍlihi* — or do they envy the people for Allah’s bounties — diagnoses the motive behind belief in idols and the reassurance that polytheists are better guided (4:51), and behind withholding even a speck if they had kingdom (4:53). *Ḥasad* — envy — was read as wishing the bounty be removed from its recipient, not merely wishing for similar bounty. The sūrah has tracked *faḍl* — bounty — as the surplus God apportions — not to be craved in another’s hand but to be asked from Him (4:32), concealed by the stingy (4:37), spent for show without belief (4:38), and donated from what He provided without harm (4:39). Here the bounty envied is the Book, prophethood, and the following that the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and his community received, a bounty the sūrah has called being made clear and guided to noble ways (4:26) and being turned toward in grace (4:27). The question *do they envy* does not seek information; it exposes that the sellers’ trade of a portion for misguidance and their wish to make believers deviate were not from lack of knowledge but from resentment that bounty came to another. The Qur’an elsewhere says envy drove many of those given the Book to wish believers back to disbelief after the truth became clear, and this verse places that wish at its root.

**Book and Wisdom and Great Authority Together**

The triad *kitāb wa ḥikmah wa mulk ʿaẓīm* was explained as the complete bounty that makes guidance effective. *Kitāb* is the inscribed limit — *ḥudūd* — the inheritance shares after debts (4:11–12), the marriage bars (4:22–23), the lawful field beyond them sought with wealth in chastity (4:24). *Ḥikmah* is the understanding that makes the Book live — the prophetic clarification that debts precede gifts, that four witnesses are required for *fāḥishah*, that earth purifies where water fails (4:43). *Mulk ʿaẓīm* is the authority that lets Book and wisdom be applied — the community, the judgment between people with fairness (4:58), and the obedience to those in authority within obedience to God and Messenger (4:59). The sūrah has shown all three in this community’s early life: the Book that makes things clear (4:26), the wisdom that guides to noble ways before (4:26), and the authority that returns trusts and judges with fairness. To have been given those three in the family of Abraham before is to know that the same three given now to this branch is not usurpation but continuity. The enviers’ claim that polytheists are better guided (4:51) is therefore not only false; it is ungrateful to the bounty their own family received in all three forms.

**Why Envy Follows the Speck**

The verse follows the rhetorical question about shares of kingdom where even a *naqīr* — speck on a date stone — would be withheld (4:53) because envy explains that withholding. If those given a portion of the Book had shares of dominion, they would not give a speck, and the reason is *ḥasad* — they begrudge the *faḍl* given to others. The sūrah has diagnosed envy as a social force before — *“do not crave what Allah gave some over others; ask Him for bounty”* (4:32) — and here it names its historical root. The cure the sūrah offered there — ask God for bounty — is the cure here as well. Instead of envying the people for what God gave, ask Him for what He gives, because the distributor is not the family that envies; it is the One who never wrongs by a *fatīl* (4:49) and who multiplies good many times over (4:40). The sūrah has also said God knows best who enemies are and is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45), so the envious wish to see believers deviate (4:44) cannot remove the bounty it envies; it can only expose the envier.
verses.55:
> Yet some believed in him while others turned away from him. Hell is sufficient as a torment

**Hell Is Sufficient as Torment**

The closing *wa kafā bi jahannama saʿīrā* — and Hell is enough as a torment — uses *kafā bi* — enough is — the same phrase that declared God enough as Guardian and enough as Helper (4:45). There sufficiency was reassurance for believers surrounded by those who trade the Book; here sufficiency is warning for those who turn away. *Saʿīr* — blaze, fierce flame — was read as the Fire that is already kindled, the blaze that consumes as *“We will burn them in the Fire”* was said for deliberate devouring and killing where *that is easy for Allah* (4:30) and as *“We will cast them into the Fire, whenever their skin is burnt We will replace it”* will be said for those who reject signs (4:56). *Kafā* — enough — was stressed as saying no additional torment is needed to prove the seriousness of envy that becomes barring; Hell suffices, and that suffices as deterrence. The sūrah has already described humiliating punishment prepared for concealing bounty (4:37) and for association not forgiven (4:48); this blaze is the same recompense named at the scale of the bounty refused. Great authority rejected meets great torment as its counterpart; the sufficiency on one side — God as Guardian and Helper — meets sufficiency on the other — Hell as blaze — showing that the community’s help and the deviator’s penalty are both assured without need for another witness.

**Why the Division Is Mentioned Here**

The verse follows the triad of Book, wisdom, and great authority (4:54) because that triad always divides. The sūrah has been dividing since it set limits — *ḥudūd* — whose keeping brings Gardens and whose crossing brings Fire (4:13–14), and since it said *“if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones and admit you to honour”* (4:31). Some among those given a portion will be among the few who are elevated — *Allah elevates whomever He wills and none is wronged even by a thread* (4:49) — while others fabricate lies against God as blatant sin (4:50). The same test now operates around the Prophet ﷺ. His presence makes the bounty visible as a person to be believed or turned from, which is why the verse names belief *in him* and turning *from him* as the two branches. The sūrah does not treat the turn as neutral; those who turn also wish others to deviate greatly (4:27), promote stinginess (4:37), and reassure disbelievers (4:51). The believers who believed in him, though few among those given a portion, join the larger *you are from one another* (4:25) — migrants and hosts who believed — and for them the sūrah has said God suffices as Guardian.

**A Sufficiency That Holds Both Sides**

Placed where it is, between the bounty to Abraham’s family (4:54) and the detailed recompense of Fire with skin replaced (4:56), this short verse holds both sides of the sūrah’s equation. Book, wisdom, and authority given become a cause for envy in some, for belief in others; Hell as blaze suffices for the enviers who bar, while multiplication of an atom’s weight and a great reward out of grace (4:40) suffice for the believers who give. The sufficiency of Hell as torment therefore does not stand alone; it stands opposite the sufficiency of God as Guardian and Helper, and opposite the sufficiency of atom-exact justice. *Kafā* in 4:45 tells the believer not to fear the traders of misguidance; *kafā* here tells the trader that the consequence is enough without addition. Between the two, the sūrah leaves the reader with the same choice it has posed since *“how will it be when We bring a witness”* (4:41): to believe in him through whom Book and wisdom came and to find Guardianship that suffices, or to turn away and find a blaze that also suffices, with no helper once condemned (4:52) and not even a speck withheld where kingdom is imagined (4:53).
verses.56:
> Surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. Whenever their skin is burnt completely, We will replace it so they will ˹constantly˺ taste the punishment. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**Those Who Reject Our Signs Will Be Cast Into Fire**

The verse states *inna alladhīna kafarū bi āyātinā sawwfa nuṣlīhim nārā* — surely those who reject Our signs, We will cast them into the Fire. After the division where some believed in him and others turned away and Hell sufficed as blaze (4:55), this verse names the content of rejection: *āyātinā* — Our signs. The sūrah has shown what those signs include in this context: verses about creation from a single soul (4:1), about orphan wealth and witnesses (4:6), about fixed inheritance after debts (4:11–12), about lawful marriage with dowry and chastity (4:24). About belief in Allah and the Last Day with donation from what was provided (4:39). To reject those signs after they were made clear (4:26) is not a casual dismissal; it is to cover what was shown. The verb *kafara* — to cover, to deny — matches the fabrication of lies against God that was called blatant sin (4:50) and the belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51). The recompense is cast — *nuṣlīhim* — the same roasting verb used for deliberate devouring where *We will burn them in the Fire, and that is easy* (4:30). The Fire is not a new threat added for this group alone; it is the prepared recompense the sūrah has named for humiliating withholding (4:37), for association not forgiven (4:48), and for envy that bars (4:55). Here it is attached directly to rejection of signs.

**Indeed Allah Is Almighty, All-Wise**

The closing *inna Allāha kāna ʿazīzan ḥakīmā* — indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise — gives the ground for both casting and replacing. *ʿAzīz* — Almighty, Mighty, invincible — was read as the power to cast into Fire and to renew skin without diminishment. Nothing restrains the execution of *“and Allah’s command is always executed”* (4:47). *Ḥakīm* — All-Wise — was read as the wisdom that places that power where rejection of signs persisted after clarity, guidance, and lightening (4:26–28). The pair appears here as it does after similar severe recompense, because the sūrah wants the reader to see that the severity is not vengeance but wise placement of might. The One who is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45) is mighty to help those who believed and did good (4:57) and mighty to cast those who rejected signs. The One who wills to make things clear and turn toward you (4:26–27) is wise to renew tasting for those who covered what was made clear. The Names therefore hold the verse between power and reason, so that the promise to believers that follows can be heard as equally assured.

**A Verse That Follows Envy and Precedes Gardens**

Placed between the sufficiency of Hell as blaze where some turned away (4:55) and the Gardens with pure spouses and vast shade where believers do good (4:57), this verse details the Fire that suffices. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened (4:28) and for whom avoidance of major sins covers lesser faults (4:31), the verse is not meant to crush but to define what major to avoid — rejection of signs after they were made clear. The sūrah therefore leaves the reader with two renewals side by side: one of skin for tasting, one of Gardens for abiding, and asks, while the signs are still with you and the choice is still to believe in him or turn away (4:55), which renewal do you seek.
verses.57:
> As for those who believe and do good, We will admit them into Gardens under which rivers flow, to stay there for ever and ever. There they will have pure spouses, and We will place them under a vast shade

**Those Who Believe and Do Good**

The verse opens with *wa alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — as for those who believe and do good — the counterpart to those who rejected signs and will be cast into Fire with skin renewed for tasting (4:56). The sūrah has defined belief in this context as trust in God and the Last Day with donation from what was provided (4:39), as belief in what was revealed confirming what was with them (4:47). As not elevating themselves but letting God elevate whomever He wills without wrong even by a thread (4:49). Doing good — *ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt* — was read as acting in the ways the sūrah has detailed: returning trusts, giving dowries graciously, honouring obligatory shares, provision to bystanders with kind speech, trade by mutual consent, and seeking reconciliation with two mediators. The pairing belief and doing good gathers the two parts of the sūrah’s ethic: the inner turn toward God who wills to make clear and turn toward you (4:26–27) and the outer deed that keeps limits inside weakness (4:28, 4:31). The verse therefore inherits all those prior acts as its content. To believe and do good here is to have lived the sūrah’s first fifty verses as worship.

**A Promise That Balances the Preceding Threat**

The verse follows the severest description of Fire with a parallel description of Gardens, so that the two renewals stand side by side. Rejected signs lead to skin renewed for tasting (4:56); belief and good deeds lead to Gardens renewed without need for replacement, with *khālidīna abadā* stressing that the abiding itself is the renewal. The sūrah has balanced promise and threat since it said *“these are the limits; whoever obeys... Gardens, whoever disobeys and exceeds... Fire, humiliating, abiding”* (4:13–14), and it keeps that balance here at the wider scale. The pairing also mirrors the sūrah’s ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) and its warning that God does not like the arrogant boaster who is stingy and promotes stinginess (4:37). To believe and do good is to have spent for God, not for show (4:38), from what He provided, believing in Him and the Last Day (4:39); the recompense for that spending is Gardens and shade and pure companionship, where spending is no longer needed. The symmetry teaches that the choice between Fire and Garden was never only about after; it was about how one handled trusts, limits, and words while *“Allah is ever Watchful”* (4:1) and *Witness over all* (4:33).

**The Human Weakness That Can Still Enter Gardens**

The promise is placed after the sūrah’s lightening — *humankind was created weak* (4:28) — and its covering of lesser faults when major sins are avoided (4:31), so that the Gardens do not seem unreachable for the weak. To believe and do good does not require the self-purification that fabricates (4:49–50) but the purification God gives — *Allah elevates whomever He wills* (4:49) — without wrong even by a thread. The small good that is never wronged but multiplied (4:40) is enough to set the multiplication and the great reward from grace in motion, and that great reward is named here as vast shade. The sūrah therefore invites the weak to see themselves in this verse: the one who returned orphan wealth with witnesses, who gave a small provision with kind speech (4:8), who traded by mutual consent (4:29), who asked God for bounty rather than craved another’s (4:32), is among those who believe and do good. For them, the rivers that flow without allotment and the shade that never thins are the counterpart to the meadow they kept shaded for others on earth. The pure spouses are the counterpart to the chastity they guarded when they could have sought *“those beyond, in fornication”* but chose the shelter instead.
verses.58:
> Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners; and when you judge between people, judge with fairness. What a noble commandment from Allah to you! Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing

**Give Back What Was Entrusted**
The verse gathers the whole of the sūrah's teaching about other people's property into one command: return what has been entrusted to its owners. The word is *amānāt*, trusts, and the sūrah has been listing them one after another. The orphan's inheritance must be handed over whole (4:2) and only after the child is tested and the handover is witnessed (4:6). A woman's dowry is hers as a gift and may not be taken back (4:4). The shares fixed for heirs are to be paid after debts and bequests (4:12). Pledges made between people are to be honoured (4:33). The sūrah has shown what happens to the man who swallows the orphan's property: he is eating fire (4:10), and the man who oversteps God's limits is handed disgrace (4:14). Commentators connect the verse with the keys of the Kaʿba and with ordinary deposits, and the point is the same in both: what belongs to someone else — a key, a debt, a testimony, a post — goes back to the one who has the right to it.

**Judge With Fairness**
The second command covers disputes. When people ask a judge, or a family asks two arbiters to mend a marriage (4:35), or an executor divides an estate, the measure is fairness: each person's share given without favour. The sūrah has prepared this by insisting that testimony be examined, since a charge of indecency needs four witnesses (4:15), and by warning against twisting words when speaking to the Prophet (4:46). The Arabic for fairness here is *ʿadl*, putting each matter in its place, and the Book praises it because a community cannot hold together when judgments follow the strong.

**Why the Two Names Fit**
The verse ends with God as All-Hearing and All-Seeing. The claimant speaks and the defendant answers; one of them is exaggerating. The village sees the handover or does not see it. God hears the words that both sides use and sees whether the money changed hands. The same sūrah has already said that God is witness over all things (4:33) and that He never wrongs anyone by even an atom's weight, multiplying every good deed instead (4:40). The verse in front of the reader is the standard for everything the sūrah legislates about money, and the two names are its guarantee that nothing is lost in the exchange. The same standard covers the money people earn from each other, which the sūrah allows only as trade by mutual agreement and forbids as devouring by falsehood (4:29).
verses.59:
> O believers! Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. Should you disagree on anything, then refer it to Allah and His Messenger, if you ˹truly˺ believe in Allah and the Last Day. This is the best and fairest resolution

**Three Obediences, One Root**
The verse commands the believers to obey God, to obey the Messenger, and to obey those in authority among them. The repetition is deliberate: the verb "obey" is stated twice and not a third time, which the scholars read as a sign that obedience to rulers and leaders stands inside obedience to God and His Messenger, not beside it. The Messenger's teaching is obedience to God because the Messenger is the one who explains what God commanded, and the Book elsewhere says that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God (4:80). Those in authority include the judges who return trusts and judge fairly (4:58) and the family arbiters appointed to mend a marriage (4:35). The sūrah has also shown that people can be ruled by something other than God: it mentions those who believe in false powers and idols and still claim to be believers (4:51), and it has named the men who want to be judged by a tyrant's court while claiming faith (4:60).

**When You Disagree, Take It Back**
The verse gives the method for disagreement in a single sentence: refer the matter to God and the Messenger. In practice that means the Book and the rulings of the one who received it, and not whoever has the louder voice or the heavier purse. The sūrah has already described the community that says "we hear and obey" over against the ones who say "we hear and disobey" (4:46), and it has said that the Messenger will be brought as a witness over his people (4:41). The matters a dispute can touch are the ones the sūrah has laid out: the fixed shares of inheritance (4:11; 4:12) after obligations and bequests (4:18), the care owed to parents and relatives (4:36), the rules governing marriage with those who lack a protector (4:25), the command not to take each other's wealth or lives wrongly (4:29; 4:30), and the duty to stay away from the great wrongs so that lesser faults are forgiven (4:31).
