Fairness requires that a man answer according to the same Book when the judgment goes against him.

**The Best Ending**
The verse closes by naming the outcome rather than the process: this is the fairest and the best in the end. The sūrah has repeated the note of ease and of God's wish to lighten burdens (4:28), the prayer allowance for those on a journey or ill (4:43), and the reminder that God knows best who your enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45). Obedience here is not blind following; the reference point is stated, and it is the Book and the man who brought it. The sūrah has shown what obedience to God means in practice: keeping the limits He set for inheritance after debts and bequests (4:13), paying the shares He named (4:12), never taking each other’s lives (4:30), and the warning that the men who cross those limits are headed for the fire (4:14).
verses.60:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who claim they believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They seek the judgment of false judges, which they were commanded to reject. And Satan ˹only˺ desires to lead them farther away

**Which They Were Commanded to Reject**

The clause *wa qad umirū a yakfurū bihi* — though they were commanded to reject it — makes the referral doubly blameworthy. *Kufr bi al-ṭāghūt* — to deny, to reject the false authority — was commanded as the counterpart to belief in God, as in *“whoever rejects ṭāghūt and believes in Allah has grasped the firm handhold”* elsewhere. The sūrah has already described belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* by those given a portion of the Book as trading guidance for misguidance (4:51) and has linked *ṭāghūt* to idols and false gods whose judgment is not *ʿadl* — fairness — as commanded for judges (4:58). To seek judgment from what you were commanded to reject is to reverse the sūrah’s ethic of referral — *refer it to Allah and His Messenger* is the best and fairest outcome (4:59) — and to choose the forum that follows desire and leads away. The sūrah elsewhere says *“do not devour wealth by falsehood”* and *“do not kill yourselves”* where *that is easy for God* (4:29–30); seeking *ṭāghūt* was read as the institutional form of that devouring, where property and life are taken by a judgment that is not mutual consent nor fairness but overstep.

**Satan Desires to Lead Them Farther Away**

The closing *wa yurīdu al-shayṭānu a yuḍillahum ḍalālan baʿīdā* — and Satan only desires to lead them farther away — names the companion behind the forum. *Ḍalālan baʿīdā* — far, distant straying — was explained as the opposite of the noble ways God wills to guide to (4:26) and of the clear path He wills to make plain. The sūrah has paired two wills before — *Allah wishes to turn to you, but those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly* (4:27) — and here Satan’s will is the deeper source of that wish. The false judge is not neutral; he is the instrument of a straying that grows with each step, as the sūrah showed where trading a portion for misguidance and reassuring disbelievers they are better guided (4:51) also had no helper once condemned (4:52). The distance — *baʿīd* — was heard as both moral and spatial: far from the limits set as *ḥudūd* (4:13–14), far from the trust returned to rightful owners (4:58), and far from the Garden whose rivers flow and whose shade is vast (4:57). The hypocrites who seek *ṭāghūt* while claiming belief think they are choosing a convenient forum; the verse says they are being led farther from the path that was made clear and lightened because they are weak (4:28).

**Claim, Referral, and Far Straying as a Sequence**

The verse traces a sequence that the sūrah has exposed in stages. That claim was already diagnosed in *“we hear and we disobey”* said as though it were *we hear and obey* (4:46). Second, the referral — *yurīdūna a yataḥākamū ilā al-ṭāghūt* — where the dispute is taken to the wrong authority, the opposite of *fa ruddūhu ilā Allāhi wa al-rasūl* (4:59). The sūrah has shown that far wandering ends in wishes to be dust and no speech hidden from God (4:42), in Fire with skin renewed for tasting (4:56), and in condemnation with no helper. To seek *ṭāghūt* is to step deliberately onto the side where *rāʿinā* is played with tongues and faith is discredited, rather than the side where *unẓurnā* is said and it would have been better and more proper (4:46).

**A Test of Belief That Is Practical**

Placed after the command to return trusts and judge with fairness and the declaration that such is a noble urging from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), and after the command to obey and refer disputes (4:59), this verse tests belief at the point where it costs. To choose the Book and the Messenger is to accept that inheritance shares after debts (4:11–12), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) will be the standard; to choose *ṭāghūt* is to seek a standard that follows desire, as those who follow desires wish you to deviate greatly (4:27). Satan’s desire to lead farther away is already at work in that will, which is why the sūrah follows this exposure with the hypocrites’ turning away stubbornly when called to the revelations and the Messenger (4:61), and with the disaster that later brings them back swearing they intended only good.
verses.61:
> When it is said to them, “Come to Allah’s revelations and to the Messenger,” you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly

**You See the Hypocrites Turn Away Stubbornly**

The response is *raʾayta al-munāfiqīna yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* — you see the hypocrites turn away from you stubbornly, barring, holding back. *Ṣudūd* doubled as verb and verbal noun — *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* — stresses stubborn barring, not a polite excuse. The hypocrites were explained as those who display belief with the tongue while preferring another judge with the heart, as in the report of a Jew and a hypocrite who disputed and the Jew accepted the Prophet ﷺ while the hypocrite sought a soothsayer. The turning is *ʿanka* — from you — personal to the Messenger ﷺ, showing that referral to the Book is inseparable from referral to him. The sūrah has said that God is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45) and that whoever takes Satan as associate has an evil associate (4:38); to turn from the Messenger to *ṭāghūt* is to choose the second companionship. The doubling *ṣudūdā* suggests both that they turn themselves away and that they bar others, as earlier they wished you to deviate greatly (4:27) and promoted stinginess (4:37). To see them turn in that way is to see the earlier diagnosis made visible: those given a portion who trade it for misguidance (4:44) and who believe in *jibt* do not merely hold an opinion; they move.

**Why the Call Exposes the Hypocrite**

The call to *“come to what Allah revealed and to the Messenger”* exposes what seeking *ṭāghūt* had concealed. A person can claim *“we believe in what was revealed to you and before you”* (4:60) while no dispute is present; the claim is cheap where it costs nothing. When a real dispute over property, marriage, or alliance requires a judgment that will give a wife her quarter or an orphan his share, the claim is tested. The hypocrite turns because the Book’s judgment will not favour the desire that sent him to the false judge. The sūrah has prepared this test since it defined trade by mutual consent (4:29) and said deliberate devouring leads to Fire that is easy for God (4:30); the hypocrite prefers the judge whose consent is to power, not to truth. The verse therefore links to 4:59’s alternative for true believers: *if you disagree, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you truly believe in God and the Last Day*. The hypocrite’s turning shows the condition was not met; belief in the Last Day where a witness is brought and nothing hidden (4:41–42) would have made him come, but he turns, because he trusts the nearer gain of *ṭāghūt* more than the distant witness.

**Turning as Barring**

The emphatic *yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdā* was read as both intransitive and transitive: they turn away and they bar. The same root *ṣadda* described those who turned away from him (4:55) — *man ṣadda ʿanhu* — where Hell sufficed as blaze. Here the hypocrites are *yaṣuddūna* — barring — implying they not only refuse to come but keep others from coming by example, excuse, or alliance with those who distort words — *we hear and disobey* (4:46). The sūrah has shown that barring is the method of those who follow desires and wish you to deviate (4:27) and of those who reassure disbelievers they are better guided (4:51). The hypocrite’s stubborn turning is therefore not a private withdrawal; it is a public barricade. The Prophet ﷺ is told *you see them* — *raʾayta* — you see it plainly, implying the turning is not hidden behind courtesy. The same community that was told to give advice that will shake souls (4:63) is first told to see the turning for what it is, so that advice is not mistaken for mere quarrel. To see is the first step of the sūrah’s handling of hypocrisy, which will add turning away from them, cautioning, and admonishing within (4:63) before any public exposure.
verses.62:
> How ˹horrible˺ will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done, then they come to you swearing by Allah, “We intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation.”

**How Will It Be When a Disaster Strikes Them**

The question *fa kayfa idhā aṣābathum muṣībatun bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* — how will it be if a disaster strikes them because of what their hands have done — mirrors the sūrah’s earlier *how will it be when We bring a witness from every community* (4:41) and *how will it be if they are struck*. *Muṣībah* — disaster, affliction that hits the mark — was read as any calamity that exposes the hypocrite’s referral to false judges (4:60) and his stubborn turning from the revelations and Messenger (4:61): defeat, exposure, punishment, or the failure of the alliance with *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* that did not help (4:52). *Bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* — because of what their hands have done — ties the disaster to their own prior acts, as the sūrah has tied Fire to deliberate devouring where *that is easy for Allah* (4:30) and humiliating punishment to concealing bounty (4:37). The question *kayfa* — how — is left hanging, as it was with the witness scene, so the listener feels the shame before it is described. Those who sought the false judge for advantage will find advantage become affliction, because the sūrah has said that the false judge’s path is Satan’s desire to lead farther away (4:60) and farther away ends in no helper.

**Because of What Their Hands Have Done**

The phrase *bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* was stressed as tying the disaster to prior choice, not to fate alone. The hands that sought *ṭāghūt* — the hands that signed, paid, or promised alliance — are the same hands to which the disaster is traced. The sūrah has tracked hands throughout: the hand that mixes orphan wealth (4:2), that reclaims a heap of gold by slander (4:20), that trades a portion of the Book (4:44), that distorts words with tongues (4:46), and that fabricates lies against God as blatant sin (4:50). Each act was done by hands that later claim goodwill. To say disaster strikes because of what hands put forward is to say recompense is continuous, as skin renewed for tasting is continuous (4:56) and as an atom’s weight of good is multiplied continuously (4:40). The hypocrites’ oath *we intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation* tries to separate intention from act, claiming a good will behind a bad referral. The verse keeps intention and act together by attributing the *muṣībah* to what hands did, not only to what hearts wished. A will that chose *ṭāghūt* over the Book and Messenger is already known — *Allah knows what is in their hearts* as the next verse will say (4:63) — so the hands’ work is the evidence of it.

**Goodwill and Reconciliation as Borrowed Language**

The words *iḥsān* and *tawfīq* in the oath are not condemned in themselves; the sūrah commends both where they are real — *iḥsān* to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36), and *tawfīq* between spouses where mediators desire harmony and God brings it (4:35). What the verse exposes is borrowed goodness after disaster, not goodwill before. To seek *ṭāghūt* for judgment is not *iḥsān* toward the community, because *iḥsān* in judgment is to return trusts and judge with fairness as a noble urging (4:58) and to refer disputes to God and Messenger as best outcome (4:59). To seek *ṭāghūt* is the opposite of *tawfīq*; it leads farther away, as Satan desires (4:60). When disaster follows — exposure, loss of trust, or defeat — to come swearing goodwill is to ask that the borrowed words cover the referral. The sūrah has already said that failure to repent until death is present is not accepted (4:18) and that turning soon is accepted (4:17); the oath after disaster is closer to the first than the second, because it comes after the hands’ work and only when the cover is needed.
verses.63:
> ˹Only˺ Allah knows what is in their hearts. So turn away from them, caution them, and give them advice that will shake their very souls

**Allah Knows What Is in Their Hearts**

The clause *ulāʾika alladhīna yaʿlamu Allāhu mā fī qulūbihim* — only Allah knows what is in their hearts — follows the oath of the hypocrites that they intended nothing but goodwill and reconciliation after disaster struck because of what their hands put forward (4:62). The oaths were *yaḥlifūna bi Allāhi* — swearing by God — yet the verse says the hearts behind the oaths are known to Him. The sūrah has prepared that knowledge: He is ever Watchful over you (4:1), enough as Reckoner (4:6), Witness over all things (4:33), All-Knowing, All-Aware where mediators desire harmony (4:35), All-Hearing, All-Seeing over trusts and judgments (4:58), and has perfect knowledge of them (4:39). To say He knows what is in hearts is to say oaths do not change the record; the hands’ referral to false judges (4:60) and the stubborn turning from the Book and Messenger (4:61) are already entered. The Qur’an elsewhere says that God knows the treachery of eyes and what breasts conceal, and that He knows the hypocrites’ excuse before it is spoken. Here that knowledge is placed at the head of the counsel, so that what follows is done with clarity: the Prophet ﷺ and the community are not told to uncover hearts by force; they are told that hearts are already known to the One who will reckon.

**Caution Them**

The second instruction *wa ʿiẓhum* — and caution them, exhort them — adds the voice of warning. *Waʿẓ* — admonition that reaches the heart, reminding of limits, Gardens. Fire — was explained as private caution that names what was done — seeking false judges though commanded to reject them, turning from the revelations and the Messenger — and what follows if it persists — condemnation with no helper (4:52), blaze enough (4:55), Fire with skin renewed (4:56). The sūrah has shown caution as part of handling ill-conduct in the home — advise them first (4:34) — and as part of the noble urging to return trusts and judge with fairness (4:58). Here caution is directed at the community’s internal ill-conduct, where hypocrisy seeks to make the Book one judge among others. To caution is to bring the hypocrite back to the referral that defines belief: come to what God revealed and to the Messenger (4:61). The caution is not public shaming but moral alert, because the One who knows hearts also wills to turn toward those who turn (4:26–27) and to lighten because weakness is real (4:28). Caution keeps that turn possible.

**Advice That Will Shake Their Souls**

The third instruction *wa qul lahum fī anfusihim qawlan balīghā* — and give them advice that will shake their very souls — was read as speech that reaches inside, *fī anfusihim* — in their selves — and is *balīgh* — reaching, penetrating, eloquent in the sense of arriving. Early authorities described *qawlan balīghā* as speech that makes the hearer fear the standing before witnesses where no statement can be hidden (4:41–42), that recalls the atom’s weight that is never wronged but multiplied (4:40). That reminds that soon repentance for ignorance is accepted while deferral until death is present is not (4:17–18). The sūrah has praised *qawlan maʿrūfā* — kind speech at distribution (4:8) — and *qawlan sadīdā* — straight speech (4:9), and here it adds penetrating speech that moves the private self.
verses.64:
> We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah’s Will. If only those ˹hypocrites˺ came to you ˹O Prophet˺—after wronging themselves—seeking Allah’s forgiveness and the Messenger prayed for their forgiveness, they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful

**Messengers Sent to Be Obeyed by Allah’s Leave**

The statement *wa mā arsalnā min rasūlin illā li yuṭāʿa bi idhni Allāh* — We only sent messengers to be obeyed by Allah’s Will — follows the counsel to turn away from hypocrites, caution them, and speak penetratingly to their souls (4:63). The verse gives the reason referral to the Messenger is not optional. A messenger is not sent to be one judge among false judges — *ṭāghūt* — whom they were commanded to reject (4:60), nor to be heard and disobeyed with distorted *rāʿinā* (4:46). He is sent *li yuṭāʿa* — to be obeyed — and that obedience is *bi idhni Allāh* — by Allah’s leave, permission, knowledge and enabling. Obedience to the Messenger is therefore not a separate loyalty but the form obedience to God takes where He has sent a clarifier. The sūrah has said to obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority within that obedience (4:59), and to refer disputes to them as best outcome. Here it explains why: the sending itself was for obedience. The hypocrites’ stubborn turning from the revelations and the Messenger (4:61) contradicts the very purpose of sending. The sūrah has shown that God wills to make things clear and guide to noble ways and turn toward you (4:26); the messenger is the clarity and the guide made a person, and to be sent to be obeyed is how the will to turn becomes practicable.

**They Would Have Found Allah Ever Accepting, Most Merciful**

The promise *la wajadū Allāha tawwāban raḥīmā* — they would have certainly found Allah ever Accepting of Repentance, Most Merciful — gives the outcome of that coming. *Tawwāb* — ever Accepting, repeatedly turning — was explained as God turning toward the servant who turns toward Him, again and again, as He turns toward those who repent soon after ignorance (4:17). *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful — was shown as the sūrah’s refrain for the weak for whom burdens are lightened (4:28) and for whom earth purifies where water fails (4:43). The pair here tells the hypocrites that the door they closed by seeking *ṭāghūt* is still the door of mercy if they come through the Messenger. The sūrah has stressed that God forgives what is below *shirk* for whomever He wills (4:48, 4:116) and that *shirk* itself is not forgiven if held to death without turning, yet the turn remains possible while breath remains and before death is present (4:18). To find Him *tawwāb* is to find that coming after wronging oneself, with *istighfār* and the Messenger’s *istighfār*, is the soon return that is accepted. The verse does not guarantee acceptance without coming; it guarantees acceptance with it.

**Why the Messenger’s Prayer Matters**

The addition of the Messenger’s seeking forgiveness — *astaghfara lahumu al-rasūl* — was read as more than courtesy. The Messenger is the witness brought over his community (4:41) and the one whose obedience is the proof of claim to believe, so his prayer for them means that their return is not isolated but rejoined to the community. Early authorities noted that the hypocrites who had sought *ṭāghūt* had broken the communal trust that disputes are referred to Book and Messenger as best outcome (4:59); to return and seek forgiveness with his prayer repairs that breach. The Qur’an elsewhere says that if the hypocrites had come seeking forgiveness, it would have been better and more proper, as straight speech would have been better than *rāʿinā* (4:46). Here the same better and more proper is enacted as movement — come, seek, have him seek — rather than as wording alone. The sūrah’s ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) and of appointing mediators where harmony is desired and God brings it (4:35) finds an echo: where the soul desires reconciliation — *tawfīq* — God brings it, and where the hypocrite desires forgiveness, the Messenger’s prayer joins, and God is found ever Accepting.
verses.65:
> But no! By your Lord, they will never be ˹true˺ believers until they accept you ˹O Prophet˺ as the judge in their disputes, and find no resistance within themselves against your decision and submit wholeheartedly

**No Faith Without the Verdict**
The verse opens with an oath, and its tone is not gentle: by your Lord, they will not be believers until they bring their disputes to the Prophet and accept his judgment — and not only with their mouths. The Arabic says they must find no tightness in themselves against what he decides; the word for that tightness is *ḥaraj*, the feeling of a chest closing over a ruling that goes the other way. And then they must submit without argument. Faith is therefore tied to the practical willingness to be judged by the Book, not only to the profession of belief in it.

**What the Sūrah Has Been Disputing About**
The disputes the verse has in view are the ones the sūrah has been regulating: who takes which share of an estate (4:11; 4:12), a dowry that was given and now is asked back, which the sūrah forbids (4:20), money earned or lost in trade (4:29), and a marriage that has cracked so badly that two arbiters have to sit down (4:35). The verse was connected by the early commentators with a quarrel between a Companion and a Jewish man; the Jewish man accepted the Prophet's ruling, and the Companion, or a hypocrite standing with him, went looking for a different judge. The verse settles where the community's cases belong.

**The Tightness the Sūrah Has Diagnosed**
The sūrah knows all about that tightness in the chest, and it names the places it comes from: craving what God has given other people and asking Him for His bounty instead (4:32), begrudging people the good things God has given them (4:54), and urging others into miserliness (4:37). The cure it offers is the reminder that God multiplies good work far beyond its weight (4:40), that He knows best who your enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), and that His will in this book is to make matters clear to people (4:26) and to forgive those who stay away from the great wrongs (4:31). Alongside the acceptance the verse demands, the sūrah has drawn the opposite picture: the men who turn away when they are called (4:61), and the men who arrive with clever words about goodwill when everything was settled (4:62). The verse in front of the reader gives the whole argument its final form: the Book is accepted in practice or it is not accepted at all. The disputes in front of the community are the ones the sūrah has been settling all along: which heir takes which share (4:12), and how property held in trust is handed back to its owner (4:58).
verses.66:
> If We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes, none would have obeyed except for a few. Had they done what they were advised to do, it would have certainly been far better for them and more reassuring

**A Hard Command They Would Not Have Borne**

The verse states *wa law annā katabnā ʿalayhim an iqtulū anfusakum aw ikhrujū min diyārikum mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum* — if We had commanded them to sacrifice themselves or abandon their homes, none would have obeyed except for a few. The sūrah has just set an oath that true belief requires accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without inward resistance and with whole submission (4:65). That oath is demanding, yet this verse says a still harder command — to kill themselves or to leave their homes — would have been obeyed by even fewer. *Anfusakum* — yourselves — was read as sacrificing their own lives, and *min diyārikum* — from your homes — as exodus, as the migrants endured when they left Makkah. The sūrah therefore measures the community against a harsher test and finds only a few would have passed, which is not condemnation of all but realism about weakness. The same weakness explained as *“humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and met with lightening (4:28) is shown here as historical fact: given a command that cut at life and home, most would have held back. The verse was linked to hypocrites who claimed belief yet turned from the Book and Messenger (4:60–61); the harder command exposes that softer claims of obedience already falter, so harder claims would have failed almost completely.

**Had They Done What They Were Advised**

The alternative *wa law annahum faʿalū mā yūʿaẓūna bihi la kāna khayran lahum wa ashadda tathbītā* — had they done what they were advised to do, it would have been far better for them and more reassuring — names the better path that was actually asked. *Mā yūʿaẓūna bihi* — what they were advised, what they were urged to do — gathers the noble urgings the sūrah has given: return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness (4:58), obey God and the Messenger and refer disputes (4:59), accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without *ḥaraj* and with *taslīm* (4:65), avoid major sins (4:31), and trade by mutual consent (4:29). None of those require leaving homes or self-sacrifice; they require keeping limits about wealth and marriage, referral to the Book, and obedience where obedience is the purpose of sending (4:64). To have done that *would have been khayr* — better — in both worlds, and *ashadda tathbītā* — more reassuring, firmer in grounding. *Tathbīt* — to make firm, to reassure — was read as inner firmness, steadiness after the wavering that marks the hypocrite who lags (4:72) and the one who fears people as God should be feared (4:77). The sūrah elsewhere says *“if you avoid major sins We will cover lesser ones and admit you to honour”* (4:31); doing what was advised is that avoidance made active, and firmness is its inner reward.

**Advice That Firms the Heart**

Placed after the oath of faith as submission (4:65) and before the promise of great reward and guidance to the straight path for doing what was advised (4:67–68), this verse is the sūrah’s pastoral diagnosis for wavering hearts. It acknowledges that a community learning to divide estates with *“whether little or much”* (4:7), to guard the orphan’s property with witnesses (4:6), and to fight in God’s cause for the oppressed (4:75) will find the commands heavy if measured against a still heavier command that only a few would bear. To have done what was advised — come to the Messenger, seek forgiveness, accept judgment, avoid major sins, trade by mutual consent — would have been better and more reassuring, not because the advised acts are small, but because they are the deeds that make the heart firm. The next verses will say that doing them brings great reward by grace and guidance to the straight path (4:67–68); this verse says they also bring *tathbīt* — firmness — now, where the hypocrite feels only the tug between claiming belief and seeking *ṭāghūt*.
verses.67:
> and We would have granted them a great reward by Our grace

**A Great Reward by Our Grace**

The promise *wa idhan la ātaynāhum min ladunnā ajran ʿaẓīmā* — and We would have granted them a great reward by Our grace — continues the counterfactual: had they done what they were advised to do, it would have been better and more reassuring (4:66). Then We would have granted a great reward — *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — from *ladunnā* — from Our presence, out of grace. The sūrah has used *ajr ʿaẓīm* before for the atom’s weight multiplied — *“We will multiply it many times over and give a great reward out of grace”* (4:40) — and for those who fight whether they achieve martyrdom or victory (4:74). Here it is the reward for doing what was advised — the ordinary urged acts of returning trusts, judging with fairness (4:58), referring disputes (4:59), and accepting the Prophet ﷺ as judge without resistance (4:65). *Min ladunnā* was stressed as grace beyond exact recompense, the same grace that makes the great reward more than multiplication. The counterfactual shows that the reward is not distant; it would have followed the advised deeds directly — *idhan* — then — without a long delay. The sūrah therefore invites the wavering to see that the great reward is not only for the hard command to sacrifice or emigrate that few would have done (4:66), but for the advised path that was within reach and was better.

**Grace That Makes the Reward Great**

The phrase *min ladunnā* was read as marking the source that makes the reward *ʿaẓīm* — great. A gift from a great giver is great because of the giver. The sūrah has already said that God never wrongs even by an atom’s weight but multiplies good and gives a great reward out of grace (4:40), and that He is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45). That sufficiency is the background to this promise: the One who is enough to help against traders of misguidance (4:45) is enough to grant. Early authorities linked *ajr ʿaẓīm* here to the Gardens promised for keeping limits (4:13), for believing and doing good with vast shade (4:57), and for obeying God and the Messenger to be in the company of the blessed (4:69). The reward is therefore not a single coin but a company and a place. The verse generalises what earlier verses specificed: the honourable entry for avoiding major sins (4:31), the Gardens with rivers for keeping limits, and the multiplication for an atom’s weight. Had they done what was advised, that entire economy of grace would have been theirs, without needing to face the harder test.

**Had They Done — The Unlived Alternative**

The *law* — had they done — frames the great reward as an unlived alternative for the hypocrites who instead sought false judges and turned away stubbornly (4:60–61). The alternative was close: come to the revelations and the Messenger (4:61), refer disputes to them (4:59), and accept judgment without *ḥaraj* (4:65). The sūrah elsewhere says *“whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of the blessed”* (4:69), and this counterfactual shows the company missed. The phrasing *la ātaynāhum* — We would have given them — with the emphatic *lām* and *qad* implied in *idhan*, was read as certainty, not hesitation. There was no doubt about the giver; the doubt was about the doers — *few would have obeyed* the hard command, and fewer still did the advised one. The great reward therefore hangs not on divine reluctance but on human doing. The sūrah has already said *“Allah does not wrong even by an atom”* and *“what harm if they had believed and donated from what was provided”* (4:39); the same logic operates: no harm would have come, and great reward would have, had the advised been done.
verses.68:
> and guided them to the Straight Path

**Guided to the Straight Path**

The promise *wa la hadaynāhum ṣirāṭan mustaqīmā* — and We would have guided them to the Straight Path — completes the counterfactual: had they done what they were advised, it would have been better and more reassuring (4:66), We would have granted a great reward by grace (4:67), and guided them to the straight path. The sūrah has used *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* as the way that God wills to make clear and to guide to — the noble ways of those before you (4:26) — the opposite of the far straying Satan desires when they seek false judges (4:60). To be guided to the straight path was explained as being shown the road and being made to walk it with firmness — *tathbīt* — the same firmness named as more reassuring in 4:66. The three results therefore form one movement: better outcome, firmer heart, great reward, and straight guidance. The path is called straight — *mustaqīm* — because it does not tilt — *mayl* — toward one wife at another’s expense (4:129), nor deviate greatly — *maylan ʿaẓīmā* — as those who follow desires wish (4:27), nor turn away stubbornly — *ṣudūd* — as hypocrites do from the revelations and Messenger (4:61). The straight path was read as the Book and the prophetic way taken together, the same pair that disputes are to be referred to as best outcome (4:59). Guidance to it is therefore not only information but enablement.

**Guidance as the Fruit of Doing**

The verse makes guidance a fruit of doing what was advised, not only of hearing it. The sūrah has warned against those who were given a portion of the Book yet trade it for misguidance and wish you to deviate (4:44) and who believe in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* and call disbelievers better guided (4:51). To do what was advised — return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness (4:58), obey and refer (4:59), accept the Prophet ﷺ as judge without inward resistance (4:65) — is the practice that keeps the path straight. Early authorities noted that *hadaynāhum* — We would have guided them — implies God’s act of guidance follows the servant’s act of obedience, as elsewhere *“those who are guided, He increases them in guidance”* and *“whoever believes in God, He guides his heart.”* The sūrah elsewhere says that avoidance of major sins leads to a honourable entry (4:31) and that an atom’s weight of good is multiplied with a great reward (4:40). Guidance to the straight path is the form that entry takes when viewed as a road. The path is straight because it was made clear — *yubayyina* (4:26) — and because it is the way of those before who kept limits; to be guided to it is to be placed among them.

**A Path That Holds After Witnesses and Before Battle**

Placed between the great reward and the company of the blessed, this verse holds the moral road between the witness scene (4:41–42) and the coming call to fight for the oppressed (4:75). The straight path that would have been granted had they done what was advised is the same path that the believers are now called to walk when they take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71). It is straight because it does not seek false judges (4:60), does not distort words (4:46), does not believe in *jibt* (4:51), and does not envy for bounty (4:54). To be guided to that path is to have the heart made firm — *ashadda tathbītā* — so that when the order to fight comes, the group that fears people as God should be feared (4:77) will not turn. When the order to give comes, the hand that was stingy will open. For the weak who were told that avoidance of major sins covers lesser ones (4:31), that promise is the straight road ahead, leading to the company that the next verses will name as the honourable fellowship of the guided.
verses.69:
> And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger will be in the company of those blessed by Allah: the prophets, the people of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous—what honourable company

**The Company of the Blessed**
The verse follows a command with a promise. Whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be with four groups: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. The Arabic for the last three carries their qualities in the names: *ṣiddīqīn* are the ones whose honesty is total, *shuhadāʾ* are the witnesses and the men killed in God's cause, and *ṣāliḥīn* are those whose lives are in good order. The early community read the promise against a report in which a man told the Prophet that he loved him and feared he would not reach his rank in the next life; the verse answered that obedience brings a person into the same company, whatever his place in the earthly queue.

**Who the Four Groups Are**
The prophets are the line the sūrah has just mentioned, the family of Abraham who were given the Book, wisdom and great authority (4:54), a line the Prophet stands in. The truthful are those whose words and conduct match; Abū Bakr was known by that title because he believed at once, and the quality is what the verse also asks of the community that was told to go out and fight and did not waver (4:77). The martyrs are those who fight in God's cause and either win or are killed, both honoured with a great reward (4:74), and witnesses whose testimony stands beside the testimony the Prophet gives for his own people (4:41). The righteous are the believers who do good and enter gardens with shade that stretches wide (4:57), the men and women who leave the great wrongs and are admitted to a free and honourable place (4:31).

**The Obedience the Verse Means**
The obedience the verse speaks of is not a general goodwill, because the sūrah has spelled out what it looks like: property returned to orphans with witnesses at the handover (4:6), dowries given to the women they belong to (4:4), marriage entered with wealth and self-restraint rather than appetite (4:24), fair and kind treatment of wives (4:19), trade by agreement and not by false dealing (4:29), and somebody stepping in when a marriage is failing (4:35). A person who keeps those things is not claiming a rank; he is walking the road the sūrah has already described (4:65; 4:66; 4:67; 4:68). The sūrah has also said that God raises whom He wills and wrongs nobody by a thread (4:49), that He multiplies good (4:40), that He knows best who our enemies are (4:45), that the men who buy error with guidance want the believers off the road (4:44), and that His will to lighten and clarify stands over the whole book (4:28). The verse in front of the reader names the company that walking that road arrives at: prophets, truthful, martyrs, righteous — and calls it an excellent company to be in. The road the sūrah has described is walked in public: the believers take their precautions and march in groups or all together when they are told to (4:71), they stand with the men, women and children who cry out for help (4:75), and they fight for God’s cause rather than for the cause of false powers (4:76). The promise attached to that road is the one the sūrah stated earlier, that the men who obey are given a great reward (4:66), that the obedient are guided to a straight path (4:67), and that the path itself is God’s gift (4:68).
verses.70:
> This is Allah’s favour, and Allah fully knows ˹who deserves it˺

**A Favour, Not a Wages Bill**
The verse is a single sentence resting on the verse before it: this — the promise of the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous — is a favour from God, and God knows the people who deserve it. The word for favour is *faḍl*, which in the Book means good that runs beyond what a person's work could require. The sūrah has already given the community both sides of this: it told people not to envy what God has given others and to ask Him from His bounty (4:32), and it described the misers who hold back God's gift and call others to miserliness (4:37), while promising the man who gives from his wealth that his good is multiplied many times over, with a great reward added by favour (4:39; 4:40).

**Favour in the Sūrah's Other Pictures**
The sūrah has used the same word for what God gave the family of Abraham: the Book, wisdom and great authority, none of it earned by the recipients (4:54). It has used it for the honour given to those who obey when it says that God raises whom He wills and wrongs no one by a thread (4:49), and it has shown how far the opposite road leads: men who invent lies about God and treat the lie as a light matter (4:50), men who take false powers and idols as their authority and then say the disbelievers are better guided than the believers (4:51). The sūrah also names two kinds of people who talk about obedience and do not mean it: the ones who want the judgment of a tyrant's court and claim to be believers in the same breath (4:60), and the ones who turn away as soon as they are called back to the Book and the Messenger (4:61). Faith without submission to the Book is not faith, as the verse with the oath said (4:65), and the man who does what he is told is then given a great reward and guided to a straight path (4:66; 4:67; 4:68).

**The Name at the End**
The verse closes with God as All-Knowing, and the sūrah has already explained that knowledge: God never wrongs anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40), He knows best who the community's enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), and He knows the difference between the man who obeys to be seen and the man who obeys because he means it (4:81 will describe the group who say "we obey" and spend the night working against it). The favour named in the verse is given where the knowledge finds the right material. The verse before this one promised the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69). The sūrah had already explained what is asked of a person and what is given in return: the men who obey are given a great reward (4:67), and the guidance to a straight path is God’s gift rather than a wage (4:68). The burden is lightened for those who carry it, since God does not ask of anyone more than he can bear (4:28).
verses.71:
> O believers! Take your precautions and go forth either in groups or together

**Take Your Precautions**

The command *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū khudhū ḥidhrakum* — O believers, take your precautions — follows the promise that obedience places with the blessed and that God knows who deserves favour (4:69–70) and calls to action. *Ḥidhr* — precaution, guard, readiness — was explained as preparation that befits the threat: arms, knowledge of terrain, counsel, and caution in movement. The sūrah has shown that precaution accompanies all trusts — witnesses at the orphan’s handover (4:6), four witnesses before sanction for *fāḥishah* (4:15), two mediators from families where a split is feared (4:35), and fairness in judgment (4:58). To take *ḥidhr* in the field is that same ethic applied to fighting. The verse generalises what earlier verses specificed for the market and the home: do not approach the weighty act without awareness. Prayer is not approached without knowing what is said or without purification, with earth where water fails (4:43); battle is not approached without guard. The sūrah has called humankind weak and promised lightening (4:28); precaution is part of that lightening, because the weak are not told to fight unwatched but to fight guarded.

**A Community That Knows Its Weakness and Its Guard**

Placed where it is, between the honourable company for obeying (4:69–70) and the portrait of laggers (4:72–73), this verse steadies the community that was learning to fight for the oppressed who cry *“deliver us, appoint for us a helper”* (4:75). The oppressed — men, women, and children — call for a *walī* and *naṣīr* — guardian and helper — the same two sufficiencies the sūrah said God alone provides (4:45); to answer that call the believers must go forth, but they must go forth with *ḥidhr*. The sūrah has paired *“Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving”* (4:43) with purification through earth, and *“and guided them to the straight path”* (4:68) with doing what was advised; here it pairs *take precautions* with *go forth* to show that courage is not carelessness. The believers who fight for God and the disbelievers who fight for the Devil with weak schemes (4:76) are distinguished not only by cause but by preparation. Those who take *ḥidhr* and go forth as commanded fight for God with the means that make fighting responsible; those who lag behind or rush without order fight for other causes or not at all. The verse therefore trains readiness as worship.

**Precaution as Obedience**

The command to take precautions was read as obedience itself, not as worldly prudence added to obedience. The Prophet ﷺ took *ḥidhr* in every expedition — scouts, guards, night watch — while trusting in God as enough as Trustee (4:81) and Witness (4:79). The sūrah’s earlier promise that *“whoever fights whether martyred or victorious We will give a great reward”* (4:74) does not remove the need for guard; it secures the meaning of guard, so that precaution is not fear but preparation that trusts. A community that learns to take precautions as commanded will not be hurried by news of security or fear that the next verses say should be referred to the Messenger and authorities (4:83). To go forth in groups or together after taking precautions is to act where the order to fight comes (4:77) with the awareness that death overtakes wherever you are, even in towers (4:78), yet *“what is with God is better and more lasting.”* The sūrah therefore makes precaution the middle between the fear that says *delay fighting* (4:77) and the recklessness that ignores *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29). Take guard, then go forth — in the form the lawful authority decides — and the weak who were promised lightening will find that the guarded going is the straight path walked.
verses.72:
> There will be some among you who will lag behind so that if you face a disaster, they will say, “Allah has blessed us for not being there among them.”

**Some Among You Will Hold Back**
The verse follows the command to be on guard and to march out in groups or all together (4:71). It says that some among you will slow down and stay behind, and then it gives the words such a man uses when a disaster hits the others: God has favoured us by keeping us out of it. The phrase "among you" matters. The shirker in the verse is not outside the community; he is inside it, close enough to be counted as one of the believers, and his attitude is what the sūrah has already called out twice: the men who claim faith and then want the case decided by a tyrant's court (4:60), and the men who turn away as soon as the Book and the Messenger are mentioned (4:61).

**Calling a Failure a Blessing**
The offence in the verse is not just staying behind; it is calling that absence a favour from God. The word for favour here is the same one the sūrah uses elsewhere with its true meaning: God's blessing is what draws a person into the company of the prophets and the truthful and the martyrs and the righteous (4:70). The shirker in the verse empties the word and hangs it on his own safety. The sūrah also shows the same tongue at work in the man who swears that he wanted nothing but the good and a reconciliation between people when the matter was over (4:62), so that a word built for God's service is turned into a shield.

**The Measure the Sūrah Gives**
The sūrah has given the community measures to check that kind of talk. God knows best who your enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45). The community that says "we hear and obey" is contrasted with the one that says "we hear and disobey", and the refusal is described as disobedience to God's command (4:46). God gives His bounty to whom He wills (4:55). The man who stays behind is set against the man who fights in God's cause and the man who sells his present life for the life to come (4:74). And the sūrah has already answered the question of whether staying home is safer, since God made all humanity from one soul (4:1) and He is the one who keeps peace or lets it be broken in a marriage (4:35). The next verse lets the same man speak again, and it is the mirror image of this one: when the bounty arrives, he wants a share, and the sūrah has already described what harm it would have done him to believe and give (4:39) and the kindness that should have ordered his dealings with parents, relatives, orphans and neighbours (4:36) in the first place. The same man speaks again in the next verse, where the bounty arrives and he wants a share of it (4:73). The sūrah’s protection of the weak runs through all of this: it has already set rules for women who have no family to defend them (4:25).
verses.73:
> But if you return with Allah’s bounties, they will say—as if there had been no bond between you—“We wish we had been there with them to share the great gain!”

**If You Return With Bounty, They Wish They Had Been There**

The verse continues *wa laʾin aṣābakum faḍlun min Allāhi la yaqūlanna ka a lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddatun yā laytanī kuntu maʿahum fa afūza fawzan ʿaẓīmā* — but if you return with Allah’s bounties, they will say, as if there had been no bond between you, we wish we had been there with them to share the great gain. The contrast with the previous portrait is deliberate: at disaster — *muṣībah* — the lagger said *Allah has blessed us for not being there* (4:72); at bounty — *faḍl min Allāh* — the same person says *would that I had been there to share*. The sūrah has defined *faḍl* as bounty to be asked from God rather than craved from another (4:32), as what the stingy conceal (4:37), and as what would have caused no harm if believed and donated from (4:39). The sūrah has called the ultimate triumph *fawz ʿaẓīm* for keeping limits (4:13) and *afūza fawzan ʿaẓīmā* is the lagger’s use for worldly gain, showing that his measure of *fawz* is gain, not Gardens.

**As If There Had Been No Bond Between You**

The clause *ka a lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddah* — as if there had been no bond between you — was explained as the lagger speaking as though he were a stranger who happened to miss a caravan, not as one among you — *minkum* (4:72) — whose absence at disaster was already a statement. *Mawaddah* — affection, bond, love — was read as the tie that should have made him go forth with them as one body, the tie the sūrah rooted in *“created from a single soul”* (4:1) and *“you are from one another”* (4:25) and appointed as heirs and as *mawālī* (4:33). To speak as if no *mawaddah* existed reveals that the bond was never acted as bond; it was kept as name while the foot stayed back. The Qur’an elsewhere says the hypocrites’ hearts are divided though you think them together; this speaking — wishing to be there only when gain is sure — proves it. The believers were told to take precautions and go forth in groups or together (4:71); the lagger who stays, then at gain says *would that I had been there*, treats going forth as a market to join when profitable, not as a duty to share. *Ka a lam takun* — as if there had never been — shows that for him the community’s *mawaddah* was conditional on outcome, which is the opposite of the *mawaddah* the sūrah asks mediators to seek where God brings harmony when desire is for repair (4:35).

**Great Gain as Worldly Measure**

The phrase *fa afūza fawzan ʿaẓīmā* — to share the great gain — was stressed as the lagger’s definition of greatness. The sūrah has called the Gardens with rivers and staying forever the ultimate triumph — *fawz ʿaẓīm* (4:13) — and martyrdom or victory in God’s cause followed by a great reward as honour (4:74). The lagger’s *fawz ʿaẓīm* is spoils, not that. To call spoils *ʿaẓīm* — great — while calling absence at disaster a blessing — *anʿama* (4:72) — shows that his great and his blessing are both measured without God as Helper whose help suffices (4:45). The sūrah will soon say *“let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in God’s cause; whoever fights whether martyred or victorious We will give a great reward”* (4:74), where *ʿaẓīm* returns as divine reward for fighting, not for wishing to have fought. The lagger’s *yā laytanī* is therefore not repentance; it is envy that the bounty came without him, as those who envy the people for God’s bounties (4:54) envied Book and wisdom given to Abraham’s family. The gain he now wants is the *faḍl* whose distribution he earlier begrudged.
verses.74:
> Let those who would sacrifice this life for the Hereafter fight in the cause of Allah. And whoever fights in Allah’s cause—whether they achieve martyrdom or victory—We will honour them with a great reward

**In the Cause of Allah**

The qualification *fī sabīli Allāh* — in the cause of Allah — was stressed to distinguish the believer’s fighting from fighting for the Devil. The next verse says *believers fight for God while disbelievers fight for the Devil, so fight the Devil’s forces, his schemes are weak* (4:76). *Sabīl Allāh* in this sūrah was shown as the clear path God wills to make plain (4:26), the noble ways of those before, the limits about wealth and marriage whose keeping is obedience. The help for the oppressed who cry *“appoint for us a saviour, a helper — all by Your grace”* (4:75). To fight in that path is to answer that cry, as the next verse asks *what is it with you that you do not fight for the oppressed men, women, and children* (4:75). The sūrah elsewhere says *“do not devour wealth by falsehood”* and *“do not kill yourselves”* (4:29) and that doing so deliberately leads to Fire easy for God (4:30). Fighting in God’s cause is the opposite taking — not devouring wealth or killing without right — but risking wealth and life for those whose wealth was devoured and whose lives are oppressed. The cause therefore gathers the sūrah’s ethic of *iḥsān* (4:36) into a field; kindness to the traveller and to those in possession becomes, at scale, deliverance for the land of oppressors.

**Whether Martyred or Victorious — A Great Reward**

The promise *wa man yuqātil fī sabīli Allāhi fa yuqt al aw yaghlib fa sawwfa nuʾtīhi ajran ʿaẓīman* — whoever fights in God’s cause, whether they achieve martyrdom or victory, We will honour them with a great reward — was read as securing both outcomes. *Yuqt al* — is killed — was explained as martyrdom — *shahādah* — the witness that joins the company of the blessed — prophets, truthful, martyrs, righteous — what honourable company (4:69). *Yaghlib* — prevails, is victorious — is the gain the lagger envied when he said *would that I had been there to share the great gain* (4:73). Here the gain is following fighting, not wishing. *Ajr ʿaẓīm* — great reward — appeared for doing what was advised (4:67), for the atom multiplied (4:40), and here for fighting whether martyred or victorious, showing that the reward is not tied to worldly outcome but to cause and resolve. The sūrah has already said *“had they done what they were advised, We would have granted great reward and guided to the straight path”* (4:67–68); fighting in God’s cause is the advised act for those whose trade is the next life, and the guidance and reward follow either way. The lagger at disaster who called absence a blessing (4:72) and at bounty who wished he had been there misses both, because he neither sold the *dunyā* nor fought.

**A Verse Between Lagging and the Oppressed’s Cry**

Placed between the portrait of wishing after gain and the cry of the oppressed, this verse turns wishing into doing. The lagger wishes *fawzan ʿaẓīmā* after (4:73); the fighter is promised *ajran ʿaẓīman* whether martyred or victorious before the outcome is known. The oppressed men, women, and children who cry for a saviour (4:75) are the reason the sale matters beyond self-gain; to sell this life is to buy deliverance for them with the help of the enough Guardian and Helper (4:45). The sūrah has shown that God never wrongs even by an atom but multiplies good (4:40) and that He fully knows who deserves favour (4:70). The fighter who sells this life knows that no sacrifice is unrecorded and that the great reward is from *ladunnā* — from His presence — as *ajr ʿaẓīm* by grace (4:67). For the community told to return trusts and judge with fairness as a noble urging from the All-Hearing, All-Seeing (4:58), fighting in that cause is the public form of returning the trust of protection to its rightful owners — the oppressed — and the recompense is the same great reward that crowns the private trusts kept.
verses.75:
> And what is it with you? You do not fight in the cause of Allah and for oppressed men, women, and children who cry out, “Our Lord! Deliver us from this land of oppressors! Appoint for us a saviour; appoint for us a helper—all by Your grace.”

**What Is It With You That You Do Not Fight**

The question *wa mā lakum lā tuqātilūna fī sabīli Allāhi* — and what is it with you, you do not fight in the cause of Allah — is not a request for information; it is a rebuke that awakens. The sūrah has just called *let those who would sell this life for the next fight in God’s cause* and promised a great reward whether martyred or victorious (4:74). Now it asks why the broader community hesitates when the cause is not only the path of God but the distress of people. The lagger who called absence at disaster a blessing (4:72) and wished to have been there at bounty (4:73) is the type for whom the question is asked; the fighter who sells this life for the next is the answer. The sūrah elsewhere says *take your precautions and go forth in groups or together* (4:71) and *believers fight for God while disbelievers fight for the Devil whose schemes are weak* (4:76); this question is the moral pressure between those two, aimed at the gap between knowing the cause and moving for it. The cause — *sabīl Allāh* — was shown as the clear path God wills to make plain (4:26), the limits about wealth and marriage whose keeping is obedience, and the help for the weak; fighting in that path here means fighting where the weak cannot fight for themselves.

**For Oppressed Men, Women, and Children**

The addition *wa al-mustadʿafīna min al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildāni* — and for the oppressed among men, women, and children — specifies whose cause is God’s cause at this moment. *Mustadʿafīn* — those made weak, deemed weak, oppressed — were explained as Muslims in Makkah and other places held under the power of oppressors, unable to emigrate or to defend. Among them were men, women, and children, the very groups the sūrah has been guarding: men and women with obligatory shares (4:7, 4:11–12), women with dowries and a firm commitment (4:19–21), children with tested competence and witnesses at handover (4:6). To fight for the oppressed of each is to bring the sūrah’s ethic of *iḥsān* — kind doing — to parents, relatives, orphans, poor, neighbours, companions, travellers, and those in possession (4:36) into the field. The Qur’an elsewhere praises delivering the oppressed as among the great acts, and the sūrah’s own logic of trusts — *return trusts to rightful owners and judge with fairness* (4:58) — becomes, at scale, deliverance for those whose trusts — freedom, property, worship — are denied.

**Deliver Us From This Land of Oppressors**

The quoted cry *alladhīna yaqūlūna rabbanā akhrijnā min hādhihi al-qaryati al-ẓālimi ahluhā* — Our Lord, deliver us from this land of oppressors, whose people are oppressors — was heard as a daily prayer of the detained, a *duʿāʾ* that names the place as *the town whose people are oppressors* rather than naming a tribe, showing that the character of its people — *ẓālim ahluhā* — makes it oppressive. The sūrah has named *ẓulm* throughout — consuming orphan wealth unjustly (4:10), devouring by falsehood deliberately (4:30), fabricating against God (4:50), and envy as *ḥasad* that withholds (4:54). To be oppressed is to live where those forms are the rule. The cry asks not only for removal — *akhrijnā* — deliver us out — but for governance after removal, which is why it continues *appoint for us a guardian and appoint for us a helper — all by Your grace* (4:75). The phrase *min ladunka* — from Your presence — matches *ajr ʿaẓīm min ladunnā* — great reward from Our presence (4:67, 4:74) — showing that the deliverance and the reward share the same source. The oppressed do not ask first for wealth or revenge; they ask for a *walī* and *naṣīr*, the two sufficiencies the sūrah said God Himself provides (4:45) and now provides through those who fight.
verses.76:
> Believers fight for the cause of Allah, whereas disbelievers fight for the cause of the Devil. So fight against Satan’s ˹evil˺ forces. Indeed, Satan’s schemes are ever weak

**Two Camps, Two Causes**
The verse separates the two sides by what they are fighting for and not by lineage or numbers. The believers fight in God's cause; the disbelievers fight in the cause of false powers, the ambitions and idols that stand in the place of God. The sūrah has made both causes concrete. On one side stands the cause that asks a person to deliver the weak who are crying out (4:75), to return what has been entrusted and to judge fairly (4:58), and to obey God, His Messenger and the men in authority among the community (4:59), accepting the Prophet's ruling without tightness in the chest (4:65). On the other side stands the cause that keeps the oppressed where they are: the old allegiances to idols and false judges (4:51), the false courts (4:60), the appetite that follows desire, and the appetite that devours other people's wealth (4:29).

**The Men Who Fight for the Second Cause**
The sūrah has already drawn the portraits of the men who serve the second cause. They are the ones who trade guidance for error and want to see the believers leave the road (4:44). They are the ones who hold back what God gave them and push others to do the same (4:37), and the ones who spend in order to be seen while not believing in God or the last day (4:38). They are the ones who talk about obedience and then spend the night undoing what they said (the sūrah's picture in 4:46 and 4:81). The Book's verdict on their patron is short: the schemes of Satan are weak. It has said earlier, in the same key, that God will multiply a good deed well beyond its weight (4:40) and that whoever follows his desires wants the believers to wander far away (4:27), and it has set that against God's will to make His religion clear and to guide people and to accept their repentance (4:26).

**What the Believers Are Told**
The verse ends with an instruction rather than a threat: fight the allies of Satan, because their planning is thin. The sūrah's fighters are the ones who take their precautions and remember God as they go (4:71), who are told that God knows best who their enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), and who know that whether they die or win, both are gain (4:73 will say it in the same passage, and 4:74 has already named the great reward). The struggle is not presented as a contest of strength but as a contest of causes, and the weaker cause is named as the one that is already losing. The two camps are distinguished by how they answer the call to the Book: the men who twist words while they pretend to agree are on the other side (4:46), and the men who fight in God’s cause know that whether they are killed or they win, the reward is secured (4:74).
verses.77:
> Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who had been told, “Do not fight! Rather, establish prayer and pay alms-tax.”? Then once the order came to fight, a group of them feared those ˹hostile˺ people as Allah should be feared—or even more. They said, “Our Lord! Why have You ordered us to fight? If only You had delayed ˹the order for˺ us for a little while!” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “The enjoyment of this world is so little, whereas the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. And none of you will be wronged ˹even by the width of˺ the thread of a date stone

**From Restraint to Command**

The verse recalls *a lam tara ilā alladhīna qīla lahum kuffū aydiyakum wa aqīmū al-ṣalāta wa ātū al-zakāta* — have you not seen those who had been told, do not fight, rather establish prayer and pay alms? — a reference to the early Makkan period when fighting was withheld and the community was commanded to worship and give. Early reports place this among believers in Makkah who asked permission to fight when oppressed, were told to restrain hands and to establish prayer and zakat instead, and then, after migration when the order to fight came, a group among them faltered. The sūrah has shown a similar pattern of lightening because humans were created weak (4:28) and of making things clear before imposing; the progression — *kiffu aydiyakum* then *qitāl* — is the sūrah’s method of preparing a community. To pray and to give are themselves preparation for fighting: prayer teaches awareness before standing (4:43) and giving teaches that wealth is trust to be circulated (4:37–38). Those who learned those two when fighting was barred would later fight for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) with the right cause — for God, not for *ṭāghūt* (4:76). The verse therefore recalls a stage where restraint was obedience, so that later fighting would also be obedience, not desire for gain that the laggers show (4:73).

**A Group Feared People as Allah Should Be Feared**

The portrait continues *fa lammā kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitālu idhā farīqun minhum yakhshawna al-nāsa ka khashyati Allāhi aw ashadda khashyah* — then once fighting was prescribed, a group of them feared people as Allah should be feared, or even more. *Khashyah* — fear that humbles and restrains — belongs to God. The sūrah elsewhere says to fear God and that He is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and that Satan’s schemes are ever weak (4:76). To fear people with that fear is to place the creature where the Creator belongs, and to fear them more is the precise reversal of *“you are from one another”* and *“Allah is Ever-Pardoning”* where earth replaces water. The fear was explained as fear of the hostile forces’ numbers, of death in fortified towers (4:78), and of losing the little enjoyment of this world (4:77). The Qur’an elsewhere says that true fear of God leads to keeping limits about wealth and marriage, while fear of people leads to seeking false judges (4:60) and to distorting words (4:46). Here fear of people leads to asking why fighting was ordered and wishing it delayed.

**The Enjoyment of This World Is Little**

The answer *qul matāʿu al-dunyā qalīl wa al-ākhiratu khayrun li man ittaqā* — say, the enjoyment of this world is little, whereas the Hereafter is far better for those mindful of God — reframes the delay request with proportion. *Matāʿ al-dunyā* — enjoyment, provision of this world — was read as safety kept by lagging, gain wished after bounty (4:73), and the heap of gold not reclaimed where the dowry was given (4:20). Each is *qalīl* — little — when set beside the Hereafter, where Gardens with rivers and vast shade await believers who do good (4:57) and where martyrdom or victory in God’s cause brings a great reward (4:74). *Li man ittaqā* — for those mindful of God — was stressed as the condition that links this verse to the sūrah’s opening *“be mindful of your Lord”* (4:1) and to *“be mindful of God and speak equitably”* (4:9). Mindfulness makes the Hereafter appear greater because the mindful see with the sūrah’s measure — *not an atom wronged but multiplied* (4:40) — rather than with the lagger’s measure — safety now. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“the Hereafter is better and more lasting,”* and the sūrah’s own division of shares — whether little or much (4:7) — is little beside the *ajr ʿaẓīm* promised for fighting.
verses.78:
> Wherever you may be, death will overcome you—even if you were in fortified towers.” When something good befalls them, they say, “This is from Allah,” but when something evil befalls them, they say, “This is from you.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Both have been destined by Allah.” So what is the matter with these people? They can hardly comprehend anything

**Death Reaches You Anywhere**
The verse answers two things said in the verses before it. The first is the request of the faint-hearted men who asked for the order to fight to be delayed a while (4:77). The second is the reasoning of the man who stayed behind and counted his absence from the battle a favour (4:72). The answer is a plain fact: death will reach you wherever you are, even if you are sitting in a fortified tower. The Arabic verb carries the sense of something that comes after you rather than something that simply happens in one place. The One who made humanity from a single soul and spread men and women across the earth (4:1) is the One who has fixed the term for each of them, and no wall delays it.

**"This Is From You"**
The second half of the verse reports the grumbling of the same people. When something good comes their way, they say it is from God; when something bad arrives, they put the blame on the Prophet. The Book's answer is that both come by God's decree, and its comment on the men is that they understand almost nothing. The sūrah has already prepared this answer. It has said that God forgives and pardons those who turn to Him and put their conduct right (4:43), that He knows best who your enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), and that messengers are sent so that people obey them by God's permission (4:64), which leaves no room for blaming the messenger for the troubles that befall the community. The lesson is stated directly a verse later: good comes from God and the harm people suffer comes from their own conduct (4:79).

**What the Sūrah Asks in the Meantime**
The verse is not fatalism; it is the end of excuses. The sūrah's instructions stand: accept the Prophet as judge without tightness in the chest (4:65), take precautions and march in groups or together (4:71), and treat serious news carefully instead of passing it on, referring it to the Messenger and the men of authority (4:83). It has told the community that God multiplies good (4:40), that His will is to make things clear (4:26), and that His favour is what raises a person into the company of the blessed (4:70). It has also shown the two faces of the men the verse is describing: the ones who come with fine words after the matter is closed (4:62) and the ones who claim the Book and then turn away (4:61). The verse in front of the reader takes the two excuses — the delay and the blame — and answers both with the term that nobody can move.
verses.79:
> Whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a messenger to ˹all˺ people. And Allah is sufficient as a Witness

**Good From Allah, Evil From Yourself**

The verse states *mā aṣābaka min ḥasanatin fa min Allāhi wa mā aṣābaka min sayyiʾatin fa min nafsika* — whatever good befalls you is from Allah and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself. This corrects the split attribution just described, where good was said to be from God but evil was said to be from the Messenger (4:78). Both good and evil befall by divine decree — *both from Allah* (4:78) — yet the secondary cause differs. Good as bounty, victory, safety, and guidance is from God as favour — *faḍl min Allāh* (4:70, 4:73) — and even an atom’s weight of it is multiplied many times (4:40). Evil as *muṣībah* because of what hands put forward (4:62) — defeat where precaution was abandoned (4:71), withholding of a share, or seeking false judges (4:60) — is from the self as deed and desire. The Qur’an elsewhere says *“whatever affliction strikes you is because of what your hands have earned”* and the sūrah has tied disaster to *bi mā qaddamat aydīhim* repeatedly. To say evil is from yourself is therefore not to deny decree; it is to name the path by which decree arrives where the servant’s choice was the vessel. The sūrah has said humankind was created weak (4:28) and burdens lightened. Where the weak follows desire — craving another’s portion (4:32), believing in *jibt* (4:51) — the evil that befalls through that following is from that self, while the good that befalls when the weak does what was advised — better, more reassuring, great reward, straight path (4:66–68) — is from God’s grace.

**We Have Sent You as Messenger to All People**

The clause *wa arsalnāka li al-nāsi rasūlan* — We have sent you as a messenger to all people — follows the correction to show the Messenger’s role in both good and evil that befalls. He is *rasūl* — sent, messenger — not the source of decree, as those who said *this is from you* (4:78) implied. The sūrah has said messengers were sent to be obeyed by God’s leave (4:64) and that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God (4:80). To be sent to all people — *li al-nāsi* — matches the sūrah’s opening *“O humanity, be mindful of your Lord who created you from a single soul”* (4:1) and its witness scene where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41). The message he brings includes the limits about inheritance after debts (4:11–12), the bar on consuming by falsehood and the permission of trade by consent (4:29), and the purification through earth where water fails (4:43). Good that befalls when those limits are kept is from God through the messenger’s clarification; evil that befalls when they are rejected is from the self that turned away stubbornly — *yaṣuddūna ṣudūdā* (4:61) — and sought *ṭāghūt*. To send him to all people is to make the means of good universally available, so that no soul can say the call to *“come to what God revealed and to the Messenger”* (4:61) was not addressed to it.

**A Balance Between Decree and Responsibility**

Placed after *both from Allah* (4:78), this verse holds decree and responsibility together without merging them. The sūrah maintains that nothing befalls except by God’s leave — towers do not prevent death (4:78) — and at the same time maintains that hands earn — laggers’ disaster talk, distorters’ *rāʿinā*, and deviators’ wish to misguide are from selves. The sūrah has shown that choice repeatedly: trading a portion for misguidance (4:44), fabricating lies as blatant sin (4:50), believing in *jibt* (4:51), and seeking false judges (4:60). Good, by contrast, is from God even as secondary cause, because the sūrah’s good — guidance to the straight path (4:68), honourable company (4:69), vast shade (4:57) — is given as *faḍl* and *ajr ʿaẓīm* from grace (4:67). The next verse will make that turning practical: whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God, and whoever turns away, the Prophet ﷺ is not a keeper over them (4:80).
verses.80:
> Whoever obeys the Messenger has truly obeyed Allah. But whoever turns away, then ˹know that˺ We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them

**Obedience to the Messenger Is Obedience to God**
The sentence is short and total: whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God. The sūrah has been building up to it. It commanded the believers to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them, and to refer disputes back to God and the Messenger (4:59). It said that messengers are sent so that people obey them by God's permission (4:64), and it made the acceptance of the Prophet's ruling, without tightness in the chest and without argument, the test of real belief (4:65). The verse in front of the reader gives the reason for all of that: the Messenger is not a second authority beside God; he is the one who delivers and applies what God sent down, so accepting him is accepting the command, and refusing him is refusing the One who sent it.

**What the Obedience Covers**
The obedience the verse speaks of is not a general respect. The sūrah has laid out its content: giving the orphan his property and keeping the handover witnessed (4:6), treating the weak and the relatives and the neighbours well (the kindness command of 4:36), returning what is entrusted to its owners and judging with fairness (4:58), earning and trading honestly rather than by false claim (4:29), and standing in the conflict for the men, women and children who cry out for help (4:75). The sūrah has also described the alternative with great care: the men who claim to believe and then want the judgment of a tyrant's court (4:60), the men who turn away the moment they are called to the Book and the Messenger (4:61), the men whose fine words cover a decision they have already made (4:62), and the men who slowed down when the marching started and then blamed the Messenger for their troubles (4:72; 4:79).

**Not a Keeper Over Them**
The second half of the verse turns from the obedience to the Prophet's own burden: whoever turns away, God did not send him as a keeper to watch over them and force them in. The Book's messengers convey and warn; the reckoning belongs to God. The sūrah has already said that God knows what is hidden in the hearts (4:63) and that the guidance of a person is in God's hand, who guides to a straight path those whom He wills (4:68). It has described the day when every community is brought with a witness, and the Prophet is brought as a witness over his own people (4:41; 4:42), and it has said that God knows best who your enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45). The verse relieves the Prophet of a burden he never had, and it leaves the men who say "we obey" and then work against it where the sūrah has already placed them, standing in front of a God who hears. The sūrah has named the knowledge that makes the difference: God knows what is hidden in the hearts (4:63), He knows best who the community’s enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45), and His will in this book is to make matters clear (4:26). It has also said that people were made from one soul and spread across the earth (4:1), that whoever obeys has obeyed God and whoever turns away is not the Prophet’s responsibility (4:80 is this verse), and that the men who say “we obey” and then work against it in the night are on record (4:81). It has described the day when the Prophet is brought as a witness over his own people (4:41), and the day when every community is produced with its own witness (4:42), and it has separated the two camps by what they fight for (4:76). The Book has also answered the grumblers who blamed the Messenger for their troubles: good is from God, and the harm people suffer comes from their own conduct (4:79).
verses.81:
> And they say, “We obey,” but when they leave you, a group of them would spend the night contradicting what they said. Allah records all their schemes. So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**The Obedience They Announce**
The verse describes the men who had just been told that obeying the Messenger is obeying God (4:80). They answer with the word of submission: we obey. Then they leave the room, and a group of them spend the night working out the opposite of what they said. The Arabic verb for that night work is *tabyīt*, the shaping of a plan after dark, out of sight of the people who heard the promise. The verse says God writes it all down. The sūrah has already described the same wordplay: men who twist the greeting they use with the Prophet and turn it into an insult (4:46), men who turn away when they are called back to the Book (4:61), and men who arrive with a solemn reference to good intention when the matter is finished (4:62).

**The Record Nobody Escapes**
The verse's answer to the night meeting is not an argument but a ledger. God records what they plan. The sūrah has already named that knowledge in several ways: God is watchful over the people in a way no one escapes (4:1), He is a sufficient reckoner for what is held in trust (4:6), He is witness over all things (4:33), and He never wrongs anyone by the weight of an atom, multiplying good instead (4:40). The men who keep their schemes quiet should know that the Book has also said God knows best who the community's enemies are and is enough as guardian and helper (4:45) and that He knows what is inside hearts (4:63). The verse tells the Prophet that the double game is not a hidden variable; it is already written, and it will be produced.

**Trust in Place of Anger**
The verse ends with an instruction: leave them and put your trust in God, who is enough to handle a person's affairs.
