The sūrah has used the same instruction where the opposition was open: the men who wanted their case judged by a tyrant's court (4:60), the men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61), and the men whose fine words covered a decision already taken (4:62). It has also reminded the Prophet that those who could have believed and given in charity would only have gained by it (4:39), that God multiplies every good deed (4:40), that the believers were told to march with whatever they had (4:71; 4:76), and that the man who fights is promised his reward whether he is killed or wins (4:84). The community is also warned against spreading every report of fear or safety without checking (4:83). The verse turns the Prophet's response from confrontation to trust, and its last name repeats the whole sūrah's premise: God sees the room after the meeting ends. The men the verse describes are the same men the sūrah has been following: the ones who say one thing in the room and another at night (4:72), the ones who hold back what God gave them (4:37), and the ones who fight for the cause of false powers when they do fight (4:76). Against all of it the sūrah has set the plain command to accept the Prophet’s ruling and to submit to it (4:65), and its reminder that good comes from God while a person’s troubles come from his own conduct (4:79).
verses.82:
> Do they not then reflect on the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies

**A Book That Does Not Contradict Itself**
The verse asks the men who were contradicting the Prophet in private a simple question: why do they not think over the Qur'an? Then it gives the test. If this book had come from anyone other than God, they would have found plenty of contradictions inside it. The argument is one a reader can check: the Book sets out family law, war, money, prayer and inheritance in the same opening sūrah, and the rules do not pull against each other.

**What the Sūrah Has Asked Them to Think About**
The question follows the men who said "we obey" and then spent the night working out the opposite (4:81). The Book offers them a long list to reflect on: the creation of humanity from one soul and the duty to guard the ties of kinship (4:1), the return of the orphan's property as it was handed over (4:6), the fixed shares for sons and daughters (4:7) and the fuller rules for heirs (4:11; 4:12), marriage entered with wealth and restraint rather than appetite (4:24) together with the protection of women who have no family behind them (4:25), the statement that God wants to make things clear and to forgive those who turn back (4:26), trade by agreement instead of devouring other people's money (4:29), the command not to envy what others hold (4:32), the promise that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40), and the rules for prayer and cleanliness (4:43).

**Why the Two Pictures Cannot Come From One Human Author**
The sūrah has also recorded the harder half of the community's life: the men who want their cases judged by a tyrant's court (4:60), the men whose fine words arrive after the matter is closed (4:62), the command to take precautions and march out (4:71), the command to fight for the men and women and children who cry for help (4:75), the difference between the two causes men fight for (4:76) and the plea of the faint-hearted for a delay (4:77). It has answered the grumblers who blamed the Prophet for their troubles (4:78) and told the community to check serious news before passing it on (4:83). A law made by a man would bend wherever his interest or his mood bent; the Book answers all of it in one voice, and the verse hands that fact to the reader as the proof. The inheritance rules state the shares (4:11) and then handle the cases where the family is more complicated than the first list covers (4:12).
verses.83:
> And when they hear news of security or fear, they publicize it. Had they referred it to the Messenger or their authorities, those with sound judgment among them would have validated it. Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy, you would have followed Satan—except for a few

**News Carried Without Checking**
The verse describes a habit that could break a community at war: reports of safety or of danger reach them, and they pass them on at once. It then gives the remedy, which is the same remedy the sūrah has already given for disputes: take the report back to the Messenger and to the people in the community who understand it, and they will find out whether it is sound. The people who can weigh a report are described as those who can search out the truth of it, and the verse says plainly that if God's grace had not been with the community, most of them would have followed Satan instead.

**Why the Habit Was Dangerous**
The sūrah has just told the believers to take their precautions and march in groups or all together (4:71), and it has shown the man who held back and then called his absence a blessing from God (4:72). A false report also does work on the side of the enemy, and the verse joins it to that man's behaviour (4:81) and to the complaint of the faint-hearted who said they feared people as God should be feared, and asked why fighting had been prescribed for them (4:77). It sits alongside the community's duty to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them (4:59) and to refer their disputes to God and the Messenger (4:64 covers the fact that messengers are sent to be obeyed). Every one of those duties assumes that the community hears the truth, and this verse protects the supply.

**The Knowledge and the Grace Behind It**
The verse's closing words keep the community humble. Reports are checked because human judgment is incomplete, and the checking itself depends on God's help. The sūrah has already said that God gives His bounty to whom He wills (4:55), that He lightens burdens because human beings were made weak (4:28), and that the men who are given knowledge are tested by it. The instructions around this verse give practice in exactly that discipline: return what is entrusted to its owners and judge with fairness (4:58), keep the two prayers and this one (4:43), and use the prayer time of a journey or illness as God allows (4:28 again in that surrounding passage). It has shown the two causes men fight for and how weak the second cause is (4:76), and it has told the community that good and hardship both come by God's decree rather than from the man who delivered the message (4:78). A community that checks its news before it speaks is a community that can be trusted with a battle, and the verse gives it both the method and the mercy that keeps the method working. The sūrah has already said that if the people had done what they were advised it would have gone better for them (4:66), and the verse before this one asked them to think the Book over and look for contradictions in it (4:82).
verses.84:
> So fight in the cause of Allah ˹O Prophet˺. You are accountable for none but yourself. And motivate the believers ˹to fight˺, so perhaps Allah will curb the disbelievers’ might. And Allah is far superior in might and in punishment

**Fight, and Answer for Yourself**
The verse addresses the Prophet alone after a passage full of hesitant men. It tells him to fight in God's cause, and then it draws the line of responsibility: he is accountable for himself and not for those who hang back. The community had been given the command to go out in groups or together (4:71) and had been told that the fighters either die or win and that both are gain (4:74). Some of them had asked for the order to be delayed (4:77), and some had stayed behind and counted their absence a favour (4:72). The verse tells the Prophet that his duty does not wait on them.

**You Are Not Responsible for Their Choices**
The sūrah has said repeatedly that the Prophet is a warner and not a keeper (the point made at 4:80). The men described in the surrounding verses had answered the call with night meetings (4:81), with excuses after the fact (4:66), and with turning away when they were invited back to the Book (4:61). The verse leaves them out of the Prophet's ledger: he carries out the command, and the men carry what they chose. What they chose has been spelled out in the same sūrah, from the law about money and marriage (4:26) that they were reluctant to accept, to the burdens God lightened for them (4:28), to the promise of gardens for those who obey (4:57), and the witness the Messenger will be called to give over his people (4:41).

**Urge the Believers**
The second command is social: stir the believers up. The Prophet is told to keep calling them to the fight in the hope that God will hold back the strength of the men who reject the faith (4:76 is the verse that divides the two causes), and the sūrah has shown what that urging looks like in practice: the men who tell others to go out, the fighters who sell this life for the next (4:74), and the men standing for the weak who cry out (4:75). Those who obey are promised a straight path (4:68) and are told that their good is not lost (4:79). The verse closes with the reminder that God's strength and His punishment are greater than anything the other side can bring, and the sūrah has been saying the same in one form or another: guidance is His to give (4:68), goodness comes from Him (4:78), and the report about a community is checked before it is believed (4:83). The sūrah has said that messengers are sent to be obeyed by God’s permission (4:64) and that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God (4:80).
verses.85:
> Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in the reward, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will have a share in the burden. And Allah is Watchful over all things

**A Share in What You Support**
The verse sets a rule about influence. A person who speaks up for a good cause — who urges someone to give, to fight, to make peace, to do right — takes a share of the good that comes from it. A person who speaks up for a bad cause — who urges someone to hold back, to keep what is not his, to harm another — carries part of the burden of what follows. The wording puts both on the same footing, and then the verse closes with the statement that God watches what people do in all of it.

**The Causes the Sūrah Has Named**
The sūrah has given the community a great deal to support and to resist. On one side stand the mediators who mend a marriage (4:35), the men who return what is entrusted and judge fairly (4:58), and the men who answer the oppressed who cry out for help (4:75) and fight for God's cause (4:74). On the other side stand the men who encourage others into miserliness (4:37), the men who urge people away from the Book (4:44 is that passage), the men who want their cases judged by a tyrant's court (4:51 is the verse about taking false powers), and the men who inflame panic by spreading every report they hear (4:81 and 4:83 together describe that traffic). The verse tells both groups that nobody stands outside the outcome of a cause he has helped along.

**Placed After the Call to Stir the Believers**
The verse follows the command to urge the believers to go out (4:84), and it generalises it. Urging someone towards a good act is a form of support, and support carries a share of the reward; urging someone into a harmful act carries a share of the burden. The sūrah has already said that out of what God gave them some people give and others hoard (4:71), and it has told the community not to let the grumblers dictate (4:72) or the night-talkers set the agenda (4:77 and 4:79 describe the plea and the answer). It has promised the obedient the company of the blessed (4:69), an atom's weight of good multiplied (4:40), and it has told the men who sided with the wrong cause that God knows best who their enemies are (4:67 covers the warning to those who hold back; 4:76 speaks of the cause they served). The verse in front of the reader turns all of that into one line: whoever backs a cause carries its result, and God sees who backed what. The sūrah has shown the other side of support in full: men who want their case judged by a tyrant’s court (4:60), men whose wish for a share in the spoil comes out only when the outcome is counted (4:73), men fighting for false powers (4:76), men blaming the Messenger for the trouble their own hands brought (4:79), and men spreading every report through the community before anyone has checked it (4:83).
verses.86:
> And when you are greeted, respond with a better greeting or at least similarly. Surely Allah is a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner of all things

**The Greeting and Its Answer**
The verse gives the community a rule for ordinary encounters. When someone greets you with peace, answer with a better greeting or at least the same one. The greeting itself in the Muslim community is the word of peace, and the verse attaches it to a reminder that God keeps count of everything.

**A Rule for a Community That Meets Constantly**
The sūrah had gathered a mixed society: immigrants from Makkah, hosts in Madinah, believers, doubters, and the men whose loyalty was for sale. The greeting became one of the small daily tests of that society. The sūrah has already told its readers to treat parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, the neighbour, the companion and the traveller well (4:36), and the greeting is the smallest coin of that duty. The men who had been told to go out and fight (4:71) and whose news was checked before it was spread (4:83) were the same men who met each other in the street every day, and the verse keeps the ordinary courtesy inside the same moral world as the law. The sūrah has also warned that the man who holds back what God gave him is a miser (4:37) and that the man who gives to be seen is not giving for God (4:39), and it has promised that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40). A greeting given well and answered better is part of that multiplication; a greeting refused is the miserliness of the tongue.

**What the Reply Says About the Community**
The rule has a practical edge. The verse makes the reply at least equal to what was given, so that no greeting dies unanswered. The sūrah has already shown how easily words were used as weapons: the men who twisted their greeting into an insult when they met the Prophet (4:46), the men who came with impressive talk after the matter was closed (4:63 is the verse where God tells His Messenger that He knows what is in their hearts), and the men whose words at night undid what they had said in the day (4:81). Against all that, the rule is equality at the very least and kindness at best. The sūrah has made people of one another by marriage and kinship (4:25) and has opened at the creation from a single soul (4:1), and the fact that the Book gives a whole rule to a greeting shows how far that brotherhood reaches: the man who greets with lies is answered with peace, the man whose loyalty is doubtful is answered with peace, and the reckoning is left to the One who keeps the count (4:40 again is the same reminder in another form). It sits well beside the earlier commands to return what is entrusted (4:87 covers the lesson of the household and the promises made to them, and the same sūrah's call to keep agreements appears at 4:73), the fair speech the community was told to use (4:9), and the warning against the mischief that spreads from the false reports the verse before it handled (4:82 and 4:83). The two verses that follow apply the rule to real fighting and real dealing (4:94 is the passage about the man who offered peace and was killed for his flock). The sūrah has told the community that God lightens what it cannot carry (4:28), that the man who held back will wish on the day of the return that he had been with the others (4:73), that the man who counted his absence from the fight a favour has already been answered (4:72), and that a person carries a share of whatever good he has supported (4:85).
verses.87:
> Allah, there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. He will certainly gather ˹all of˺ you together on the Day of Judgment—about which there is no doubt. And whose word is more truthful than Allah’s

**There Is No God Except Him**

The verse opens with *Allāhu lā ilāha illā huwa* — Allah, there is no god worthy of worship except Him — the same declaration that the sūrah placed at the root of worship: *worship God and associate none with Him* (4:36) and *association is not forgiven* (4:48). The sūrah has shown what association looks like in practice — belief in *jibt* and *ṭāghūt* (4:51), seeking judgment of false judges though commanded to reject them (4:60), and saying to one who offers peace *you are no believer* for gain (4:94). To say *lā ilāha illā huwa* is to deny those rivals at the level of worship, judgment, and truth. The phrase follows the command to answer greeting with better or same and the reckoning of all things by the Vigilant Reckoner (4:86) to remind that the Reckoner is the only God to be worshipped. The sūrah elsewhere pairs *lā ilāha illā huwa* with *there is no helper* (4:48) to show that the One who alone is to be worshipped is the One who alone suffices as Guardian and Helper (4:45). Here the declaration stands as the premise for what follows: He who alone is God is the One who will gather.

**He Will Certainly Gather You on the Day of Judgment**

The promise *la yajmaʿannakum ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati lā rayba fīhi* — He will certainly gather all of you together on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt — was read as the gathering that the previous witness scene required. *Yajmaʿannakum* — will gather you — with emphatic *lām* and *nūn* was explained as the muster where a witness is brought from every community and the Prophet ﷺ as witness over his (4:41), where those who denied and disobeyed will wish to be dust and will not hide any statement (4:42). Where every soul that tasted death — even in towers (4:78) — is brought. The Day was called *yawm al-qiyāmah* — Day of Standing — because all stand before the Reckoner who counts even a better greeting (4:86) and an intercessor’s share (4:85). *Lā rayba fīhi* — no doubt about it — was stressed as removing the doubt that made a group fear people as God and ask *why have You ordered us to fight, delay us* (4:77) and that made laggers call absence a blessing (4:72). The One who is Vigilant Reckoner over all things (4:86) is the One who will certainly gather all things.

**About Which There Is No Doubt**

The clause *lā rayba fīhi* was linked to the Qur’an’s opening — *“this is the Book, no doubt in it”* — and to the sūrah’s question *do they not reflect on the Qur’an? Had it been from other than God they would have found many inconsistencies* (4:82). To have no doubt about the Day is the fruit of reflecting on the Book that has no inconsistency; the Book that governs inheritance whether little or much (4:7), dowry not reclaimed (4:20–21), and trade by mutual consent (4:29) without contradiction is the same Book that promises the gathering without doubt. The sūrah has shown doubt’s practical fruit: publicising news of security or fear without referral (4:83), seeking *ṭāghūt* though commanded to reject it (4:60), and distorting *rāʿinā* (4:46). Each is a doubt about whether the Book and Messenger can handle the affair. To say *no doubt about it* is to answer that doubt at its root: the gathering where every atom is weighed and multiplied (4:40) is as sure as the Book’s coherence, because both are from the same One.
verses.88:
> Why are you ˹believers˺ divided into two groups regarding the hypocrites while Allah allowed them to regress ˹to disbelief˺ because of their misdeeds? Do you wish to guide those left by Allah to stray? And whoever Allah leaves to stray, you will never find for them a way

**Why Are You Split Over Them?**
The verse asks the believers why they had divided into two groups about the hypocrites — one group treating them as Muslims still to be helped, the other treating them as enemies already. The verse's own answer is the heart of it: God has turned those men back into their unbelief because of what they did, and no one can guide a person whom God has left to wander. The question was not a request for information. It told the community that the argument itself was the problem.

**What the Dispute Was**
The sūrah has already given the evidence on both sides. These men claimed faith by day and worked against it at night (4:81). They wanted their cases decided by a tyrant's court and still called themselves believers (4:60), and they turned away as soon as they were called back to the Book and the Messenger (4:61). They came with fine words after the matters were settled (4:62), and their loyalty followed their advantage (4:72). On the other side, the community had been given clear instructions about how to treat them: check serious news instead of spreading it (4:83), return what is entrusted and judge fairly (4:58), answer a greeting with a better one (4:86), and remember that it was God's mercy that kept them from following Satan (4:87 states the same in the closing of that passage). A community with those instructions did not need to argue about the men; it needed to apply the rule and leave the judgment to God.

**The Men Who Cannot Be Guided**
The verse's last sentence is the one that settles the argument: those whom God has left to wander will find nobody to put them on the road. The sūrah has said what earns that state: taking false powers as authorities (4:51), inventing lies about God and treating them lightly (4:50), claiming a position God gives to whom He wills (4:53; 4:54 describes the family of Abraham and the gift given to them). It has also said what God does for the people who come to Him with a sound heart: He makes matters clear (4:26), He guides those who turn to Him (4:68), He gives His favour where He knows it belongs (4:54 again in the argument), and He is not unjust in the smallest degree (4:29 in the general sense). The two groups in the verse were arguing about men God had already described; the answer was to stop treating the enemy's friends as a matter of taste, and the verses that follow set out the rule for the men who wanted the safety of both sides (4:94 in this sequence, and 4:89 and 4:90 immediately after this verse). The sūrah has shown the same men twisting the words of their greeting (4:46) and ignoring the command to obey God, the Messenger and the men in authority among them (4:59). It has told the community to fight for the men, women and children who cry out for help (4:75), and it has said that the harm people suffer comes from their own conduct rather than from the man who brought the message (4:79).
verses.89:
> They wish you would disbelieve as they have disbelieved, so you may all be alike. So do not take them as allies unless they emigrate in the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take any of them as allies or helpers

**They Want You to Be Like Them**
The verse describes the wish of the men who had drifted back to unbelief (4:88): they wanted the believers to disown the faith as they had done, so that everyone would be level again. The Book has recorded that wish before in this sūrah: the men who follow their own desires want the believers to wander far away (4:27), and the men who were given a share of the Book traded guidance for error and want the same for the believers (4:44). What they wanted was for the community to abandon the rules that protected the weak and the obedience that joins a person to the company of the blessed (4:69).

**The Test: Take Them as Allies Only If They Move**
The verse gives a practical test for the community's relationship with them: do not take them as allies or protectors unless they leave their homes for God's cause, as the first believers had done when the command came (4:66). The same sūrah has praised the men who left their homes and endured the hardship of it (4:25 speaks of the believing women who migrated and the protection given to them), and it has told the community to march out and to fight for the men and women and children who could not defend themselves (4:75). The migration was the visible proof that a man had put the community before his clan.

**When They Refuse**
The verse's last part tells the community what to do with those who turn away after that test: they are to be treated as enemies in the field, seized and fought wherever they are found, and no one is to take them as ally or helper. The permission sits in the middle of a passage about war: the two causes men fight for (4:76), the command to the Prophet to fight even if others hold back (4:84), the men who only wanted the safety of both sides (4:91 describes that third group), and the rules that follow for a killing by mistake (4:92) and for a deliberate killing (4:93). The sūrah has also fixed the limits: men who come within a treaty with another people are not to be touched (4:90), those who want no part of the fighting are left alone, and the man who offers a greeting of peace is not to be called an unbeliever for the sake of a quick gain (4:29 is the general ban on taking what is not yours). The verse's severity has a boundary drawn around it in the very next line, and the community is not free to widen it. The sūrah has named the men who wanted the believers to go back with them (4:88), the men who took false powers as authorities (4:51), the men who denied the signs (4:56), and the men who were told to obey God, the Messenger and their leaders (4:59) but would not march when the order came (4:71) while keeping their eyes on the gains (4:73).
verses.90:
> except those who are allies of a people you are bound with in a treaty or those wholeheartedly opposed to fighting either you or their own people. If Allah had willed, He would have empowered them to fight you. So if they refrain from fighting you and offer you peace, then Allah does not permit you to harm them

**The Exception That Holds the Line**
The verse follows a command to seize the men who wished the community to disbelieve with them (4:89), and it carves out two exceptions. The first covers men who have taken refuge with a people who have a treaty with the believers; the community is bound by that treaty in the same way a marriage is bound by its firm pledge (4:21 is where the Book calls the marriage agreement a serious covenant). The second covers men who have come to the believers with no stomach for fighting either against the believers or against their own people. The verse says that if God had wanted, He could have given those men the upper hand, and it ends with the rule that if they stay out of the fight and offer peace, the community has no way against them.

**Why the Rule Is Stated This Way**
The exception keeps the community's word. The sūrah began by commanding the return of everything entrusted (4:58 describes the trust command and the fair judgment that goes with it), and the Book treats a treaty as one of those trusts. To honour an agreement with one people means sparing the man who is under their protection, even when he shares the ideas of the enemy. The second exception takes account of real distress rather than loyalty: the verse describes men whose hearts are too tight to fight either side, and the sūrah has used the same word for the tightness that a person feels when a decision goes against him (4:65 is where the Book demands that the heart be free of that tightness in accepting the Prophet's ruling). These men are not pretending to a faith they do not hold, like the men who wanted a tyrant's court while calling themselves believers (4:60), and they are not the men who promised peace and then broke it. The sūrah has already called for honesty in speech (4:29 covers the ban on taking other people's wealth by falsehood, and the same standard applies to promises) and for the answering of a greeting of peace with a better one (4:86).

**Where the Community Is Left**
The verse's last words are the most important: God has not given the community any way against these men. That closes the matter. The permission to fight in this passage applies to the men who wish the believers to disbelieve with them (4:88 covers the split over them and God's verdict), the men who turned back to hostility whenever they got the chance (4:89), and the men whose duplicity was exposed (4:63 is where God tells His Messenger He knows what is hidden in hearts). It does not apply to the man under a treaty, nor to the man who withdraws and offers peace. The Book elsewhere says that God watches over everything (4:45 is the reminder that God knows best who the enemies are), and the sūrah has taught the community to fight for the weak who cry out (4:75) and to answer the people who wanted peace with peace (4:28 again in the same spirit of lightening burdens). The verse keeps the two requirements together: the community defends itself against the men who attack it and keeps faith with the men who do not. The Book’s aim with the community is to make matters clear to them and to guide them (4:26).
verses.91:
> You will find others who wish to be safe from you and their own people. Yet they cannot resist the temptation ˹of disbelief or hostility˺. If they do not keep away, offer you peace, or refrain from attacking you, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them. We have given you full permission over such people

**Men Who Wanted the Safety of Both Sides**
The verse describes a third group after the double-dealers (4:88) and the men who turned to hostility whenever the chance came (4:89). These men wanted to be safe from the believers and safe from their own people at the same time, and the verse says that whenever they were drawn back into the fighting, they plunged in headlong. The test the verse gives is the same as the one in the previous verses: if they stay clear of the fight, offer peace and hold their hands, then the community leaves them alone.

**Where the Test Comes From**
The community had been told to march when it was told to march (4:71) and to stand behind the men, women and children who were being crushed (4:75), and the Prophet had been told to keep urging the believers even when the community hung back (4:84). In that setting, the man who wants the protection of both sides is a danger to the weak he claims to stand with. The sūrah has already warned about half-loyalty: the men who came with fine words after the decision (4:61), and the men who claimed to believe and wanted a tyrant's judgment (4:58 describes the trust and the fair judgment that the community owed instead). The verse separates hesitation from duplicity: the man who cannot bring himself to fight is left in peace (4:90 is the rule that protects him), while the man who keeps rejoining the fight against the believers whenever he can is treated as what he is.

**Fighting When the Line Is Clear**
The verse ends with the community being told to fight these men wherever they are found, and it says the warrant for it is clear. The Book's word for the pressure that drives a man back to the wrong side appears three times in the Qur'an with three senses: as the fighting that keeps people from the faith (2:193 is the verse that commands fighting until that pressure ends), as a test that people are to each other (25:20 states the same), and as the trial that came to a people and their garden (68:17 is that parable). A man who returns to hostility every time the pressure rises has chosen his side, and the community is allowed to treat him accordingly. The permission is bounded by the three signs the verse names — keeping away, offering peace, holding the hand — and the sūrah has already drawn the limits of that fighting: the believer does not kill a believer by design (4:92 comes immediately after), and the man who withdraws entirely is not to be attacked (4:90). The verse before this one and the one after it together show that the Book prizes the community's safety and its word at the same time. The sūrah has spoken already of the ban on taking other people’s property (4:29), of the men who traded guidance for error (4:44), and of the fact that God knows best who the community’s enemies are (4:45).
verses.92:
> It is not lawful for a believer to kill another except by mistake. And whoever kills a believer unintentionally must free a believing slave and pay blood-money to the victim’s family—unless they waive it charitably. But if the victim is a believer from a hostile people, then a believing slave must be freed. And if the victim is from a people bound with you in a treaty, then blood-money must be paid to the family along with freeing a believing slave. Those who are unable, let them fast two consecutive months—as a means of repentance to Allah. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**No Believer Kills a Believer**
The verse states a rule with one exception: it is not for a believer to kill another believer, except by mistake. Then it sets out the remedy for the mistake. If the killer causes the death without meaning to, he frees a believing slave and pays compensation to the family of the dead man, unless the family gives up the money as an act of charity. If the man killed was a believer living among people at war with the community, the killer frees a believing slave. If the man killed was under a treaty with the community, the compensation is paid to his family and a believing slave is freed. If a person has nothing, the sūrah says, then two months of fasting one after the other, with God's acceptance of his turning back.

**Why the Rule Comes Here**
The verse sits inside a passage about fighting. The community had just been given permission against the men who turned back to hostility (the previous verse, and 4:89 for the rule that came before it), and the sūrah's instructions allow a man to be fought and killed in the field; this verse puts a wall around the fighting itself. The Book calls the killing of a soul a defiling of the earth (2:30 describes the human being's appointment on the earth and the wrong that follows) and it says that the killing of one soul is like the killing of all of humanity (5:32 is that statement). The sūrah has stated the same thing in its own way: it forbade the taking of life and property by false means (4:29) and it laid down the rules of inheritance and marriage as matters of what belongs to whom, with the same seriousness (4:1 opens the law section, and 4:21 speaks of the covenant of marriage). The men who kill their own people by mistake still owe a repair: the slave freed, the money paid, the family's loss acknowledged.

**The Compensation and the Family**
The rule protects a man's family as well as his life. The money is paid to the family of the dead man, and the family may give it up; the Book has already told the community to return what belongs to others and to judge honestly (4:58), and it says that the community's duty to keep faith extends even to the case where the dead man was not a Muslim but lived under an agreement with them. God's acceptance of the man's turning back stands at the end of the verse, and the sūrah has repeated that note throughout: the burdens were lightened because human beings are weak (4:28 is the verse that says it), and God's mercy is offered to the men who repair what they have done. The verse that follows takes away that mercy for the deliberate killer, so the two verses together mark the line the Book draws around the blood of the believers. The verse sits inside a passage about war and its limits: the previous verse described the men who kept returning to the fight (4:91), the verse after this one names the deliberate killer (4:93), and the sūrah had already called the marriage agreement a serious covenant (4:21) to show how it treats obligations between people.
verses.93:
> And whoever kills a believer intentionally, their reward will be Hell—where they will stay indefinitely. Allah will be displeased with them, condemn them, and will prepare for them a tremendous punishment

**The Deliberate Killing**
The verse names the consequence for the man who kills a believer on purpose: the fire, staying in it, with God's anger on him, God's curse on him, and a massive punishment prepared for him. The Book joins the deliberate killing of a believer in several places to the worst human wrongdoing. The sūrah of the Criterion, for instance, puts the murder of a soul God has made sacred up against calling on other gods for help (25:68 states the three together), and the sūrah in front of the reader has already said that God does not forgive the man who dies joining others with Him (4:48 is that statement), and it has said that God is not unjust in the least degree (4:29 in the surrounding law, and 4:44 for the warning to the men who turn away from the Book).

**The Four Statements in the Sentence**
The verse stacks its four threats so that no reader can take the offence lightly: the fire, God's anger, God's curse, and a great punishment. The sūrah has used each of these in other contexts to make the contrast with the obedient: it promised the men who obey God and His Messenger the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69), it promised gardens that last (4:57 is the promise of the gardens under which rivers flow), it promised men and women who do good an honourable reward (4:13 is the promise attached to the limits of inheritance), and it opened the chapter's own account of the reward at 4:1 with the call to be mindful of God. Set against those promises, the four threats describe the exact opposite of the community the Book was building.

**The Argument the Teachers Made**
The early teachers argued about whether the deliberate killer had any route back. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the verse was among the last passages sent down on the subject and that nothing after it set its rule aside (Bukhārī; Muslim carry the report). The sūrah itself gives the men who follow the wrong way a warning in the same tone: they took false powers for judges (4:51 is that passage), they invented lies about God (4:54 relates to the same argument), and they were told that God's forgiveness is not offered to the man who dies in that state. The verse comes immediately after the rules for accidental killing (4:92) and immediately before the rule about the man who offers peace and is killed for his goods (4:94), and the placement is deliberate: the law protects blood, and it protects the words of peace. The sūrah has described the men cursed for their rebellion (4:118), the repentance that is accepted only before death arrives (4:17), the mercy that lightens burdens for people who were made weak (4:28), the men who traded guidance for error (4:44), the men condemned by God and left without a helper (4:52), the duty to fight for the oppressed (4:75) and the two causes for which men fight (4:76), the men who came back to hostility (4:89), and the double-faced men the community was allowed to fight (4:91).
verses.94:
> O believers! When you struggle in the cause of Allah, be sure of who you fight. And do not say to those who offer you ˹greetings of˺ peace, “You are no believer!”—seeking a fleeting worldly gain. Instead, Allah has infinite bounties ˹in store˺. You were initially like them then Allah blessed you ˹with Islam˺. So be sure! Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what you do

**Check Before You Fight**
The verse tells the believers that when they set out to fight for God's cause they are to prove what they are doing before they act, and it names the case that prompted the rule. A man came to them offering the greeting of peace, and they told him he was no believer, because they wanted the property he had with him. The verse refuses that bargain and reminds them that God has plenty to give. It adds a second reason for restraint: the men it was written about had themselves been in the same position before God blessed them with faith. It closes with the instruction to make sure, and the reminder that God is fully aware of what people do.

**The Incident the Verse Answers**
The rule was not a theory. The reports describe a man from the tribe of Sulaym, named in some accounts as Mirdās, who greeted a Muslim patrol with the greeting of peace and was killed anyway so that the men could take his flock. The Prophet was grieved by it and recited this verse, and the two main collections carry the account (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4591; Muslim 3025 in similar wording for the same theme). The sūrah had already given the community the rule for words of peace: a greeting is to be answered with a better one or at least the same (4:86 is that command), and the man who offers peace in the field is not to be touched (4:90 covers those who withdraw, and 4:91 covers the men who go back to fighting). The verse gives the community the discipline that makes those rules real: a claim of belief is not to be tested by the size of a man's herd.

**What the Reminder Adds**
The verse's reminder about the community's own past is its gentlest argument. These men had been unbelievers themselves until God's favour reached them, and the Book says the same thing to the whole community in other places (3:103 is the passage that reminds the believers how they were on the edge of a pit before God brought them together). The sūrah has been saying it in its own way from the beginning: it told the believers not to take each other's property by false means (4:29), it warned them against wanting what others hold (4:32), it promised that an atom's weight of good is multiplied (4:40), and it described the men who wanted the believers to go back to disbelief with them (4:88 is that passage, and 4:93 is the verse just before this one). The verse in front of the reader turns all of it into a single instruction for the man on the road with a weapon: be sure of what you are doing, because the goods of this world are small (4:77 says the same about the enjoyment of this life) and God has better stored up (the promise of ranks and forgiveness at 4:95 and the reward that follows it). The sūrah has already spoken of the burdens God lightens (4:28), of the men who would rather the believers disbelieved with them (4:44), of the company promised to the obedient (4:69), and of the rule that news of war is checked before it is spread (4:83). The verses around this one carry the same theme of blood and its limits: killing by mistake (4:92), killing on purpose (4:93), the rule this verse lays down itself (4:94), the ranks of the men who struggle in God’s cause (4:95), and the forgiveness and mercy they are promised (4:96).
verses.95:
> Those who stay at home—except those with valid excuses—are not equal to those who strive in the cause of Allah with their wealth and their lives. Allah has elevated in rank those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who stay behind ˹with valid excuses˺. Allah has promised each a fine reward, but those who strive will receive a far better reward than others—

**Not Equal — Those Who Stay and Those Who Strive**

The verse states *lā yastawī al-qāʿidūna mina al-muʾminīna ghayru ulī al-ḍarari wa al-mujāhidūna fī sabīli Allāhi bi amwālihim wa anfusihim* — those who stay at home among believers, except those with valid excuses, are not equal to those who strive in the cause of God with wealth and lives. *Qāʿidūn* — those who sit, stay — was explained as remaining behind from going forth in groups or together as commanded (4:71). *Ghayru ulī al-ḍarari* — except possessors of harm, of valid excuse — was read as blindness, illness, lameness, or need that prevents going forth. The phrase was reported to have been inserted after the first revelation when Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind companion, asked about his excuse and the Prophet ﷺ received the addition (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2832). *Mujāhidūn* — strivers — with *amwālihim wa anfusihim* — wealth and lives — was explained as the two expenditures the sūrah has praised: spending from what God provided (4:39) and offering this life for the Hereafter in fight for the oppressed (4:74–75). It is to rank the acts, as the sūrah has ranked obedience that places with the prophets and truthful (4:69) above disobedience that will be burned (4:14).

**Elevated in Rank — Darajah Above Those Who Stay**

The rank *faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna bi amwālihim wa anfusihim ʿalā al-qāʿidīna darajatan* — God has elevated in rank, preferred, those who strive with wealth and lives above those who stay, by a degree — was explained as a degree of closeness and reward. *Darajah* — rank, degree — was read as the standing given to the striver who verified before fighting (4:94) and who fought where trusts and justice are guarded (4:58–59). The sūrah has used degree language elsewhere where envy of God’s bounties was condemned (4:54) and where God’s favour upon the Prophet ﷺ is great (4:113); here the degree is not of envy but of effort. Early reports noted that the striver who goes forth light or heavy is not the same as the one whose excuse keeps him, though both believe; the former bears the cost that earlier only few would have borne had God commanded to sacrifice selves or abandon homes (4:66). The degree is therefore proportioned to the cost that the lightened burden (4:28) still leaves: to give wealth where stinginess is a temptation (4:37) and to risk life where death will overtake even in fortified towers (4:78).

**A Verse That Ranks Without Breaking Brotherhood**

Placed after verification before killing and the warning against seeking fleeting gain by denying peace (4:94), this ranking prevents the opposite error: that staying is the same as striving where striving is required. The sūrah has already distinguished the lagger who stays and then envies (4:72–73) from the one who offers life for the Hereafter (4:74); here it distinguishes the excused stayer from the striver, promising good to both then preferring the striver by degree and mighty wage. The ethic is the sūrah’s own: *“those who believe and do good We will admit into Gardens”* (4:57), yet within good there are ranks. For the community divided into two groups about hypocrites (4:88) and commanded to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse steadies judgment: do not equalise what God made unequal, and do not condemn whom God excused. The sūrah’s leniency for weakness — *“He wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak”* (4:28) — remains, even while wealth and lives are asked where the oppressed cry for a helper (4:75). The next verse will describe that mighty wage as ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him, the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:96).

The assurance *wa kullan waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā* — Allah has promised each a fine reward, the beautiful — was explained as the promise to both sitter with excuse and striver: Paradise for faith held, as the sūrah promised Gardens under rivers for those who believe and do good (4:57) and as it said gift and debt precede inheritance yet the limits are from God (4:11–13).
verses.96:
> far superior ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — And God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — repeats the same two names that seal the removal of mistake by fasting as repentance (4:92) and the reminder that you were as they were (4:94). *Ghafūr* — All-Forgiving — was explained as forgiving the striver’s faults where verification was imperfect yet sincere. Forgiving the sitter with excuse whose harm kept him home. *Raḥīm* — Most Merciful, ever Merciful — was read as the mercy that gave ranks from Him and that made Hijrah wide for the oppressed (4:100). The pairing after ranks shows that the whole elevation is inside mercy, not outside it. The sūrah has said *“God does not wrong even an atom, and if it is good He multiplies”* (4:40), and *“if you avoid major sins We absolve lesser”* (4:31): forgiveness and mercy are the mechanism of that multiplication where the good is striving with wealth and life. Where the intentional killer was sealed with anger, curse, and mighty preparation (4:93), the striver — and by inclusion the excused sitter promised *ḥusnā* (4:95) — is sealed with forgiveness and mercy.

**Degrees Are Gift, Not Contract**

The wording *minhu* was read by grammarians as partitive and honorific: ranks that are *from Him* — originating with Him, bestowed as gift, not bargained as wage. That matches the sūrah’s language where the great reward for doing what was advised is *by Our grace* (4:67), where the good deed multiplied is *from His grace* (4:40), and where guidance to the Straight Path is a gift after reward (4:68). To strive with wealth and life where the oppressed cry (4:75) is costly, yet the verse says the cost does not purchase rank as trade purchases goods by mutual consent (4:29). It receives rank as gift from the One who created from a single soul and spread humanity (4:1) and who wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28). The striver’s wealth, given against stinginess (4:37) and hoarding (4:39), is therefore not a loan repaid with interest but an offering answered with degrees whose distance only the Giver measures. That is why the verse leaves the number unnamed: between two degrees is as between heaven and earth in reports, yet the text keeps the eye on source — *minhu* — rather than count — so that striving is not calculated as profit but trusted as bounty.

**A Short Verse That Holds the Sūrah’s Weight Together**

Though only *“ranks, forgiveness, and mercy from Him, and God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful,”* the verse carries the sūrah’s weight. It follows the prohibition against consuming wealth unjustly (4:29) with the call to spend wealth for God where the oppressed cry (4:75). It follows the command to verify before fighting (4:94) with the assurance that verification’s owner gives ranks; it follows the distinction between sitting and striving (4:95) with the answer that the distinction is not enmity but mercy’s distribution. The sūrah opened by creation from a single soul and commanded mindfulness of ties (4:1), showed envy of God’s bounties as the disease (4:54). Taught that good and evil are from His decree while evil from the self as means (4:79); here the medicine is named as forgiveness and mercy from Him that make degrees real yet keep brotherhood. For the weak for whom burdens were lightened, the triad is the lightest yet highest: where life and wealth are given, He gives degree; where fault remains, He forgives; where nothing more can be offered, mercy carries. The next passage will turn from those who strive to those who claim oppression while remaining, whose excuse angels will interrogate (4:97).
verses.97:
> When the angels seize the souls of those who have wronged themselves—scolding them, “What do you think you were doing?” they will reply, “We were oppressed in the land.” The angels will respond, “Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?” It is they who will have Hell as their home—what an evil destination

**Those Who Wronged Themselves — At the Taking of Souls**

The verse opens *inna alladhīna tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikatu ẓālimī anfusihim* — when the angels seize, take fully, the souls of those who have wronged themselves. *Tawaffā* — to take in full — was explained as the angels’ taking at death, the same taking that will gather all upon a Day about which there is no doubt (4:87). *Ẓālimī anfusihim* — wrongers of themselves — was read as those who abandoned what preserved them, not those wronged by another. As the sūrah said *“whoever does evil or wrongs themselves then seeks forgiveness will find God All-Forgiving”* (4:110), wronging the self is the description of sin that remains with the doer, not imposed from outside. The image is the sūrah’s moral audit at the border: the angels — the same who record schemes by night (4:81) and who bring witness against communities (4:41) — seize the wronger while his claim is still *“we were oppressed.”* The taking is the moment where claims are tested, as the sūrah has shown that God knows what is in hearts (4:63) and that He is Reckoner of all things (4:86).

**Their Home Is Hell — What an Evil Destination**

The verdict *fa ulāʾika maʾwāhum Jahannam wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — It is they who will have Hell as their home, refuge, what an evil destination, becoming — was read with *maʾwā* — refuge, shelter — inverted: the refuge they sought among the hostile becomes Hell as refuge. *Sāʾat maṣīrā* — evil as destination, as becoming — was explained as the sūrah’s closing formula for the abode of those who remain where belief cannot be lived, matching *“Hell is sufficient as torment”* (4:55) and the threat for intentional killing and for siding with wrong (4:93, 4:109). The contrast with the previous tier is exact: those who strive with wealth and lives are given ranks, forgiveness, and mercy (4:96); those who stay claiming oppression while the earth is wide are given Hell as home. The distinction is not that every stayer is condemned — the next verse will exempt the truly helpless who cannot find a way (4:98) — but that the claim of weakness is audited at soul-taking. Where the sūrah earlier absolved those with valid excuse who stay behind from striving (4:95), here it condemns those whose excuse was a wide earth left unused.

**A Verse That Turns Geography Into Moral Responsibility**

Placed after ranks and mercy for strivers (4:96), this verse turns geography into responsibility. The sūrah that began with a single soul spread across lands (4:1), that promised earth spacious for emigration (4:100), and that taught that good and evil are both destined while evil from the self as means (4:79), here makes the earth’s width the measure of the excuse. To wrong oneself by remaining where the oppressed cry for a helper (4:75) when the earth is wide is not weakness but choice hidden as weakness. The angels’ question — *fī ma kuntum* — and the reply — was not God’s earth spacious — will be heard again where the community is asked why it does not fight for the oppressed; the answer in both is movement. For the weak for whom the sūrah lightens, the next verses lighten further: the helpless who truly cannot afford a way are excepted. It is right to hope God will pardon them (4:98–99), while the one who does emigrate finds refuge and abundance and, if death overtakes him on the way, his reward secured with God, the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).
verses.98:
> Except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out—

**Except the Helpless — Al-Mustaḍʿafīn**

The exception *illā al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildāni* — except helpless men, women, and children — qualifies the verdict that those who remained claiming oppression while earth is wide will have Hell as home (4:97). *Mustaḍʿaf* — deemed weak, reckoned oppressed, held down — was explained not as moral weakness but as lack of means: those judged weak by circumstance, not those who chose weakness where a way existed. The sūrah has used the same root where the oppressed men, women, and children cry for a saviour (4:75); there the cry was a reason to fight for them, here the same class is a reason to excuse them. To name *men, women, and children* was read as comprehensive: not only fighting men are assessed. Women and children whose movement depends on others and whose legal capacity the sūrah has guarded throughout — in dowry (4:4), in inheritance (4:7–11), in marriage limits (4:3), and in the command to return trusts and judge fairly (4:58). Where 4:97 counted those who wronged themselves by staying when they could leave, this verse counts those who are truly *mustaḍʿaf* and therefore did not wrong themselves by staying because staying was not chosen.

**A Verse That Holds Two Judgments Together**

The brevity — *“except helpless men, women, and children who cannot afford a way out”* (4:98) — was read as the sūrah’s balance between two judgments that might otherwise collide. The first judgment is mobility as duty where the earth is wide: *“Was Allah’s earth not spacious enough for you to emigrate?”* (4:97). The second is mercy that does not burden beyond capacity: *“God wishes to lighten”* (4:28), *“do not kill yourselves, God is ever Merciful”* (4:29), *“if you avoid major sins We absolve lesser”* (4:31). To hold both, the sūrah inserts this exception between threat and hope: the threat remains for those who could find *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* and did not, while the hope remains for those who truly could not. The construction also mirrors the earlier distinction between those who stay with valid excuse — *ulū al-ḍarar* — who are promised *ḥusnā* though not equal to strivers (4:95), and those who stay claiming oppression when excuse is absent. Here the women and children are named explicitly because the sūrah earlier quadrupled the weight of infant and female weakness in inheritance and dowry law; their explicit exemption shows that the law that guards the weak also excuses them.

**A Light Verse That Makes the Next Mercy Intelligible**

Though a fragment — five words in Arabic besides the categories — the verse makes the next mercy intelligible. Without it, *“it is right to hope God will pardon them”* (4:99) would have no subject; with it, the hope has precisely these — men, women, children without *ḥīlah* or *sabīl*. The sūrah’s ethic — return trusts, judge fairly, verify reports (4:58, 4:83), be sure before fighting (4:94), and do not confuse permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93) — is here extended to the judgment of the remaining: verify inability, then except. For the weak the sūrah lightens, this is the lightest of sentences: where you truly could not afford device and could not find a way, the evil destination does not attach, and the next verse will place your case under hoped pardon from the Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving. The verse after that will show the opposite face: the one who could find device and way and did emigrate finds many refuges and, if death meets him on the way, his reward secured with the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (4:100).
verses.99:
> it is right to hope that Allah will pardon them. For Allah is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving

**It Is Right to Hope That God Will Pardon Them**

The verse states *fa ulāʾika ʿasā Allāhu a yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — for those, it is right to hope, perhaps, maybe, that God will pardon them, will efface their sin. *ʿAsā* — to hope, to be expected, perhaps — was explained with attention because it follows an exception for the truly helpless (4:98) after a threat of Hell for those who wronged themselves while earth was wide (4:97). When *ʿasā* is from God about Himself, commentators said it carries certainty — His hope is not doubt but a gracious promise phrased as hope to keep both fear and longing alive. The sūrah has sealed other pardons with certainty: *“if you avoid major sins We absolve”* (4:31), *“whoever does evil then seeks forgiveness will find God All-Forgiving”* (4:110), and the striver’s forgiveness as ranks (4:96). Here the phrasing is softer, as befits the helpless whose case is known to God and who remain under His mercy. *Yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — to pardon them, to wipe away, to efface — was read as *ʿafw* — effacement, removal of trace — distinct from *maghfirah* — covering. *ʿafw* removes the record as if it were not written, while *maghfirah* covers it from consequence. The pronoun *ulāʾika* — those — refers precisely to the men, women, and children who cannot manage stratagem nor find a way (4:98), not to those who could and did not emigrate.

**For God Is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu ʿafuwwan ghafūrā* — For God is Ever-Pardoning, All-Forgiving, ever effacing, ever covering — was explained as the suitability of the names to the case. *ʿAfuww* — Ever-Pardoning, much effacing — recurs where an error might be held: where approaching prayer in impurity is taught (4:43) it is sealed *ʿafuwwun ghafūr*, and here where helplessness might still be judged as shortcoming. The sūrah has paired *Ghafūr Raḥīm* for strivers (4:96) and for error requiring fasting (4:92); here the pair is *ʿAfuww Ghafūr*, emphasising that pardon for the helpless is not only not punishing but wiping the sin of staying. Classical notes added that the sequence *mustaḍʿafīn* (4:98) → *ʿasā yaʿfuwa* (4:99) → spacious earth for emigrant (4:100) teaches conduct: the helpless hope, the able move, and the Pardoner covers both according to what was possible.

**A Verse That Keeps Fear and Hope Together**

Placed between the evil destination for those who wronged themselves while able (4:97) and the spacious earth promised to the emigrant (4:100), this verse keeps fear and hope together without confusing them. It does not declare the helpless forgiven as a flat verdict, lest staying become light; it does not leave them under threat, lest mercy be despaired. The phrasing *ʿasā* was understood to move the heart to keep seeking means — *ḥīlah* and *sabīl* — even while hoping, and to keep the community fighting for the oppressed who cry for a helper (4:75) rather than abandoning the helpless to their excuse. The sūrah elsewhere says *“God wills to lighten burdens, humankind was created weak”* (4:28) and *“God does not wrong even an atom”* (4:40); hope for pardon here is that lightening applied to geography — where earth is wide yet unreachable for these, pardon is hoped wide as well. The sūrah has also shown that doing what was advised would have been better and would have brought great reward (4:66–67): for the able that advice was emigration, for the helpless the advice is to remain under hope and to seek means where means appear.
verses.100:
> Whoever emigrates in the cause of Allah will find many safe havens and bountiful resources throughout the earth. Those who leave their homes and die while emigrating to Allah and His Messenger—their reward has already been secured with Allah. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Whoever Emigrates Finds Many Refuges and Abundance**

The verse opens *wa man yuhājir fī sabīli Allāhi yajid fī al-arḍi murāghaman kathīran wa saʿah* — whoever emigrates in the cause of God will find in the earth many safe havens and bountiful resources, spaciousness. *Saʿah* — spaciousness, abundance, ample provision — was read as breadth of earth and of rizq, the same spaciousness the angels cited — *was not God’s earth spacious enough?* (4:97) — now answered as found. The sūrah has shown that the oppressed cry for a deliverer from the land of oppressors (4:75) and that the helpless who cannot find *ḥīlah* or *sabīl* are hoped to be pardoned (4:98–99); here the one who can find device and way and uses them finds not desert but refuge and abundance. The verse generalises emigration beyond the historical Hijrah from Makkah: the Hijrah to Madinah after its conquest was declared ended — *lā hijrata baʿda al-fatḥ* (Bukhārī 3080; Muslim 1353) — yet the broader hijrah — abandoning what God forbade, *al-muhājir man hajara mā nahā Allāhu ʿanhu* (Bukhārī 10) — remains, and for it the promise of many havens still holds wherever a land permits God’s worship.

**And God Is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

The seal *wa kāna Allāhu Ghafūran Raḥīmā* — And God is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful — was explained as the suitability to both clauses: forgiving the emigrant’s past sins in the land left, faults in the manner of leaving. The incompleteness of a journey cut by death; merciful in giving many havens where one was expected and in securing reward where death intervened. The same pair sealed the pardon hoped for the helpless (4:99) with *ʿAfuww Ghafūr*, and the striver’s ranks (4:96) with *Ghafūr Raḥīm*; here again *Ghafūr Raḥīm* covers both Movement and mortality. The sūrah has said *“God does not wrong even an atom. If it is good He multiplies”* (4:40) and *“had they done what they were advised it would have been better and would have brought great reward”* (4:66–67); emigration is that advice made spatial, and the multiplication is many havens and secured wage even when death cuts short. The pairing also shows that emigration is not presented as heroic autonomy but as forgiveness and mercy received: the emigrant does not earn spaciousness by might; He finds it because the Ever-Forgiving opens it.

**A Verse That Answers the Angels’ Question With Geography and Grace**

Placed after the angels’ *“was not God’s earth spacious enough?”* (4:97), the exception for the helpless (4:98), and the hope for pardon (4:99), this verse answers the question with geography and grace. To those able to devise and find a way, the answer is *yajid* — you will find — many havens and abundance; to those whose way was cut by death, the answer is *waqaʿa ajruhū* — reward secured. The sūrah that opened from a single soul spread across earth (4:1) and that said God wills to make clear, to guide to noble ways. To turn in mercy (4:26–27), now makes clear that the earth’s width is not an abstraction but a set of actual refuges where prayer can be shortened without fear (4:101) and where the burdens lightened for the weak (4:28) are lightened further by place. The ethic extends beyond place to intention: the emigrant to God and Messenger is secured even without arrival, as the martyr is secure even without victory — *whether they achieve martyrdom or victory We honour with great reward* (4:74). For the community commanded to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94), the verse lightens departure: you will find refuge and abundance, and if death finds you first, your wage has already fallen upon the One who never wrongs.

**Actions Are Judged by Intentions**

The Prophet ﷺ drew the distinction this verse depends on: "Actions are by intentions, and the emigrant's reward is according to what he emigrated for" (al-Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907). Migration for God and His Messenger is therefore complete in the intention, not in the arrival, so a man who dies on the road is credited with the journey he meant. The same report adds the other side: whoever migrates for some worldly gain, or for a woman to marry, gets exactly what he migrated for. Here intention is the whole difference between travel and emigration.
verses.101:
> When you travel through the land, it is permissible for you to shorten the prayer—˹especially˺ if you fear an attack by the disbelievers. Indeed, the disbelievers are your sworn enemies

**When You Travel — Permission to Shorten the Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun a taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — when you strike through the land, travel through earth, there is no blame, no sin upon you to shorten the prayer, to curtail it. *Ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi* — striking through land — was explained as journeying, the same phrase used for struggling in God’s cause (4:94) and now widened to any travel, as the sūrah has just promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) and wide earth to those asked at soul-taking (4:97). *Fa laysa ʿalaykum junāḥ* — no blame — was read as permission, not sin, to shorten; the sūrah has used *junāḥ* for law’s ease where dowry is adjusted by mutual consent (4:24), where a wife fears indifference and settlement is sought (4:128). Where no sin attaches. *An taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāti* — to shorten from the prayer — was explained as the four-rakʿah prayers — Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, ʿIshāʾ — shortened to two, while Maghrib and Fajr remain. The practice was shown by the Prophet ﷺ on travel before fear was present, establishing that the permission is general, as ʿUmar asked why shorten when now safe and the Prophet ﷺ replied: *“it is charity that God has given you, accept His charity”* (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 686). The sūrah that wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28), that taught purification with earth where water lacks (4:43), now lightens prayer itself within spacious earth.

**Especially If You Fear an Attack by the Disbelievers**

The condition *in khiftum a yaftinakumu alladhīna kafarū* — if you fear that those who disbelieve may attack you, may tempt you, may put you to trial — was explained as fear of *fitnah* during travel, where the hostile who do not offer peace may assault the worshippers. *Yaftinakum* — to put to trial, to attack, to seduce from worship — matches *fitnah* as strife and hostility (2:191–93) and as the temptation to which the double-faced are plunged whenever returned (4:91). The phrase *“especially if you fear”* in translation was read to mark the occasion that occasions the permission most clearly, not to limit it to danger alone; the Prophet’s shortening even without enemy present shows the condition is illustrative, as travel itself brings *fitnah* of hardship, exposure, and the need for vigilance. The sūrah has described the oppressed who cry for a helper from the land of oppressors (4:75) and the permission to seize the hostile who refuse peace (4:89–91). Shortened prayer is the worship that fits that terrain where worshippers must remain armed and vigilant, as the next verse will detail with ranks of prayer while armed (4:102). The condition also teaches that fear does not cancel prayer but reshapes it, as remembrance remains standing, sitting, lying down when prayers are finished (4:103).

**Indeed the Disbelievers Are Your Sworn Enemies**

The seal *inna al-kāfirīna kānū lakum ʿaduwwan mubīnā* — indeed the disbelievers are — were — your clear, sworn enemies, manifest foes — was explained as reason for the permission and for the caution that follows. *ʿAduww mubīn* — clear enemy — was read as open hostility, not hidden envy only. The sūrah has said God knows best who enemies are and is enough as Guardian and Helper (4:45), and here the clarity of enmity is declared so that the traveller does not treat the hostile as neutral. *Kānū* — they were — was read as timeless trait of that hostility where disbelief hardens into fighting, as the Devil’s schemes are weak yet still must be curbed (4:76) and as Satan is the accursed enemy who said he will mislead (4:118–19). The manifest enmity does not contradict the exception for treaty and for the constricted who offer peace (4:90); it defines the default of the hostile collective where no treaty or peace holds. For the weak for whom burdens are lightened, the declaration is a protection: to shorten prayer when traveling is not laxity but realism about a clear foe, and to keep guard while praying (4:102) is not suspicion but obedience to the notice that enmity is manifest.
verses.102:
> When you ˹O Prophet˺ are ˹campaigning˺ with them and you lead them in prayer, let one group of them pray with you—while armed. When they prostrate themselves, let the other group stand guard behind them. Then the group that has not yet prayed will then join you in prayer—and let them be vigilant and armed. The disbelievers would wish to see you neglect your weapons and belongings, so they could launch a sweeping assault on you. But there is no blame if you lay aside your weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness—but take precaution. Indeed, Allah has prepared a humiliating punishment for the disbelievers

**When You Are With Them and Lead Them in Prayer**

The verse opens *wa idhā kunta fīhim fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta fa l-taqum ṭāʾifatun minhum maʿaka wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — when you, O Prophet, are among them and you establish prayer for them, let one group stand with you while armed and let them take weapons. *Kunta fīhim* — you being among them, campaigning with them — was explained as the Prophet ﷺ present on expedition, leading the force that earlier was told to go forth in groups or together (4:71) and to be sure before fighting (4:94). *Fa aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāta* — you establish prayer for them — was read as the prayer whose shortening was just permitted for travel (4:101), now given its battle form: the *ṣalāt al-khawf*, prayer of fear. *Ṭāʾifah* — group, party — was explained as a portion of the force dividing into two: one prays with the Imam while armed, the other faces the enemy. *Wa l-yākhudhū asliḥatahum* — let them take weapons — was stressed: even in prayer the sword is not laid aside, because disbelievers are your clear enemies (4:101) and would wish to see weapons neglected. The sūrah that promised many havens to the emigrant (4:100) now shows prayer itself finding haven in ranks while still armed.

**They Wish to See You Neglect Weapons and Belongings**

The motive *wadda alladhīna kafarū law taghfulūna ʿan asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum fa yamīlūna ʿalaykum maylatan wāḥidatan* — the disbelievers would wish you neglect, be heedless of weapons and belongings. They could sweep, assault upon you in one sweep — was explained as the enemy’s wish for a single heedless moment. *Waddū* — they wish — matches the regressed who wish you disbelieve as they have (4:89) and those who wish you deviate greatly (4:27); here the wish is tactical: that you be *ghāfil* — heedless. *Asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum* — weapons and belongings, goods — was read as the two vulnerabilities of a travelling force: arms and baggage. *Maylatan wāḥidah* — one sweeping assault, one inclination — was explained as a single rush while heads are bowed. The warning makes the prior armed prayer intelligible: the Devil’s schemes are weak (4:76) yet the human enemy remains a clear foe (4:101) who watches for neglect. The sūrah has shown that those given a portion wish to trade guidance and make you deviate (4:44); here the wish is more concrete — to find you without sword and without guard on the brow of prayer.

The ease *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum in kāna bikum adhan min maṭarin aw kuntum marḍā a taḍaʿū asliḥatakum wa khudhū ḥidhrakum* — no blame if you lay aside weapons when overcome by heavy rain or illness. Take precaution — was explained as the law’s lightening where rain soaks and weight exhausts or wounds prevent bearing. *Adhan min maṭar* — harm from rain — was read as heavy, cold rain that makes holding arms a hardship, as *ḥaraj* — constriction — in religion was removed where ablution with earth replaces water (4:43). The pairing shows the sūrah’s method: God wills to lighten burdens because humanity is weak (4:28) yet does not lighten to heedlessness. Where the sūrah elsewhere says *lā junāḥ* for settlement where a wife fears indifference (4:128) and for shortening prayer (4:101), here *lā junāḥ* permits laying arms aside without permitting neglect.

**The Fear Prayer as It Was Prayed**

The exchange this verse describes was performed in the Prophet's lifetime in several forms. The reports of al-Bukhārī (413) and Muslim (842) preserve the shape of the fear prayer: one group stands with the Imam for a rakʿah while the other faces the enemy, then the groups change places and the second prays a rakʿah with him. The scholars read these forms as the verse carried out in practice rather than left as theory. In each version the same logic holds: worship is not postponed because danger is present, and vigilance is not dropped because worship is in progress.
verses.103:
> When the prayers are over, remember Allah—whether you are standing, sitting, or lying down. But when you are secure, establish regular prayers. Indeed, performing prayers is a duty on the believers at the appointed times

**When the Prayers Are Over — Remember Standing, Sitting, Lying**

The verse states *fa idhā qaḍaytumu al-ṣalāta fa adhkurū Allāha qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — when you have finished, completed the prayer — the fear prayer just described (4:102) — then remember God standing, sitting, lying on sides. *Qaḍaytum* — completed, fulfilled, finished — was explained as ending the formal prayer with its bows and prostrations, the shortened travel form (4:101) and its guarded ranking. *Fa adhkurū* — then remember, mention, invoke — was read as keeping remembrance after the guarded rank disperses. That prayer does not end as awareness. *Qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — standing, sitting, upon sides — was explained as all postures, the same triad used where those given understanding remember God in all states and reflect (3:191). The sūrah has shown that even in the fear prayer one group stands guard while the other prostrates (4:102) and that vigilance remains even when weapons are laid aside in rain or illness; remembrance in all postures is the inward counterpart to that outward vigilance. The verse was also linked to the emigrant’s many havens (4:100): whether moving standing, resting sitting, or fallen on sides from wound, the remembrance accompanies.

**But When You Are Secure — Establish Regular Prayers**

The clause *fa idhā aṭmaʾnantum fa aqīmū al-ṣalāta* — but when you are secure, tranquil, established, then establish the prayer — was explained as returning to full prayer when fear lifts and place is secure. *Aṭmaʾnantum* — you are secure, at rest, hearts at rest — matches the security opposite the fear that shortened prayer (4:101) and that required the guarded rank (4:102). The sūrah has used *iqāmah* throughout for prayer established at its time, after purification with earth where water lacked (4:43), and as witness before God (4:41). Where the emigrant found many havens and abundance (4:100), security is the haven for prayer itself, allowing it to stand at its full height.

**The Writ That Holds the Sūrah’s Discipline Together**

The final writ — *kitāban mawqūtā* — was read as the sūrah’s discipline. The chapter has commanded returning trusts and judging fairly (4:58), referring disputes to God and Messenger (4:59), verifying reports (4:83), being sure before fighting (4:94), and not confusing permission over hostility with permission over believers (4:92–93). Prayer at fixed time is the training that makes those commands possible: it punctuates the day with reference, divides travel and fear into measured intervals, and returns the community from the rank to the standing, sitting, lying remembrance. The verse therefore closes the passage on prayer that began with purification where water lacked (4:43) and will later meet the judgment passage where the Book was sent to judge by what He has shown (4:105): both begin with a writ — purity and time — that secures justice.

The phrase was linked to *ḥāfiẓū ʿalā al-ṣalawāt* — guard the prayers (2:238) — and to the Prophet’s teaching that the prayer has appointed openings and closings.
verses.104:
> Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy—if you are suffering, they too are suffering. But you can hope to receive from Allah what they can never hope for. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**Do Not Falter in Pursuit of the Enemy**

The verse opens *wa lā tahinū fī ibtighāʾi al-qawmi* — do not falter, do not weaken, do not flag in seeking, pursuing, going after the people — the enemy. *Tahinū* — to be weak, to waver, to lose heart — was explained as slackening after the strain of travel, fear prayer. Guarded worship just taught (4:101–103). *Ibtighāʾ* — seeking, pursuing — was read as following after, not merely defending where attacked but seeking the hostile that refuses peace (4:89–91) and that wishes you neglect for a sweep (4:102). The prohibition was understood as addressed to a community that had been told to go forth in groups or together (4:71), to fight for the oppressed who cry (4:75), and whose struggles had included Uḥud’s wound and the questioning *“why was fighting ordered now and not delayed a little?”* (4:77).
